# pbt user guide (v0.5.1)

> The user guide of pbt, a property-based testing library for Go, in one file. The index of the documentation is https://go.ymotongpoo.com/pbt/guide/llms.txt.

---

# Getting started

pbt is a property-based testing library for Go. A property is a test that must hold for every input of some shape. pbt generates the inputs, shrinks a failing one to a small case, and saves that case so that the next `go test` run replays it. The feature set follows Erlang's [PropEr](https://proper-testing.github.io/): generators whose distribution you control, statistics to check that control, stateful and parallel command testing, state machines, targeted search, and existential properties.

This guide describes pbt v0.5.1. It assumes that you write tests with `go test`. The [package documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/go.ymotongpoo.com/pbt) is the reference for every function; the chapters here explain how the pieces fit together and which one to reach for.

## Install

```sh
go get go.ymotongpoo.com/pbt@v0.5.1
```

pbt needs Go 1.25 or later and has no dependencies outside the standard library. Import it as `go.ymotongpoo.com/pbt`.

## A first property

A property is a function that receives a `*pbt.T`, draws values from generators, and reports a failure through the methods it shares with `*testing.T`. `pbt.Check` runs it.

```go
// largest returns the largest element of a non-empty slice.
func largest(xs []int) int {
	m := xs[0]
	for _, x := range xs[1:] {
		if x > m {
			m = x
		}
	}
	return m
}

func TestLargest(t *testing.T) {
	pbt.Check(t, func(t *pbt.T) {
		xs := pbt.SliceOfN(pbt.Int(), 1, -1).Draw(t, "xs")
		if got, want := largest(xs), slices.Max(xs); got != want {
			t.Fatalf("largest(%v) = %d, want %d", xs, got, want)
		}
	})
}
```

Three things happen in this test.

- `pbt.SliceOfN(pbt.Int(), 1, -1)` is a generator of slices with at least one element and no upper bound. A generator is a value of type `pbt.Gen[V]`; you can store it in a variable and reuse it.
- `Draw(t, "xs")` produces one value for the current test case. The label names the value in the report of a failure.
- `pbt.Check(t, prop)` runs the property 100 times. The size parameter grows from 1 to 42 over the run, so the first cases are small and later ones larger. Chapter 3 explains the size.

`*pbt.T` has `Errorf`, `Fatalf`, `Logf`, `Cleanup` and the other reporting methods of `*testing.T`, so a property reads like an ordinary test. A panic inside the property counts as a failure too.

## When a property fails

The next implementation has a bug: it starts the maximum at 0, which is wrong when every element is negative.

```go
// biggest starts from 0, which is wrong for a slice of negative numbers.
func biggest(xs []int) int {
	m := 0
	for _, x := range xs {
		if x > m {
			m = x
		}
	}
	return m
}

var biggestProperty = func(t *pbt.T) {
	xs := pbt.SliceOfN(pbt.Int(), 1, -1).Draw(t, "xs")
	if got, want := biggest(xs), slices.Max(xs); got != want {
		t.Fatalf("biggest(%v) = %d, want %d", xs, got, want)
	}
}
```

The guide's test runs `biggestProperty` with `Seed(1)` and `NoSave()` to capture this report:

```text
[pbt] property failed after 12 passed checks and 20 shrink steps (size 13)
[pbt] xs (SliceOfN(Int(), 1, -1)) = []int{-1}
[pbt] error: biggest([-1]) = 0, want -1
[pbt] reproduce: go test -run 'TestBiggest' -pbt.seed=0x1
```

Read it line by line.

- The first line says how many cases passed before the failure, and how many shrink steps it took to reach the case shown. The failing case was found at size 13.
- Every value the property drew is listed with its label, its generator and its value. The slice that failed first had 13 elements; the shrinker removed all but one and reduced that one to the smallest negative number. `[-1]` is the smallest input that still fails.
- The `error:` line is the message passed to `Fatalf`. Log lines, panics and the output of `OnFail` callbacks appear here as well.
- The last line is the command that reproduces the run, seed included.

Without `NoSave`, pbt also saves the case under `testdata/pbt`, in a directory named after the test. The next run replays it before generating new cases. Keep that file as a regression case after fixing the bug.

## What the rest of the guide covers

The chapters build on each other. Chapters 1 to 4 cover generators, the size and distribution of the data, shrinking, and the options of a run. Chapters 5 to 7 cover stateful testing against a model, parallel execution and state machines. Chapter 8 covers targeted search and existential properties, and chapter 9 the generators derived from types. Chapter 10 covers the strings in the formats that standards define. Chapter 11 points to the examples, the migration guide for rapid users and the reference material. [Chapter 12](12-agents.md) gives coding agents a method for testing a project, from choosing properties to reporting a reproducible bug.

---

# Generators

A generator is a value of type `pbt.Gen[V]`. It knows how to produce a `V` from the choices that pbt records for the current case, and that record is what makes shrinking and replay work. You never build the record yourself: you combine generators and draw from them.

## The built-in generators

| Values | Generators |
| --- | --- |
| Integers | `Int`, `IntRange`, `IntMin`, `IntMax`, `IntRangeToward`; `Int32`, `Int64`, `Uint`, `Uint32`, `Uint64`, `Byte` and their `Range` forms; `Integer[I]` and `IntegerRange[I]` for any integer type |
| Floats | `Float64`, `Float64Range`, `Float32`, `Float32Range` for finite values; `AnyFloat64` adds NaN and the infinities |
| Text | `Bool`, `Rune`, `RuneIn`, `String`, `StringN`, `StringOf`, `StringOfN`, `StringMatching`, `Bytes`, `BytesN` |
| Time | `Time`, `TimeRange`, `Duration`, `DurationRange`, `FixedZone`, `Zone` |
| Network | `IPv4`, `IPv6`, `Addr`, `AddrIn`, `Prefix`, `AddrPort` for `net/netip`, and `HardwareAddr` |
| Collections | `SliceOf`, `SliceOfN`, `SliceOfDistinct`, `SliceOfNDistinct`, `MapOf`, `MapOfN`, `Permutation` |
| Choice | `Just`, `SampledFrom`, `OneOf`, `Frequency`, `Ptr` |
| Functions | `Func`, `Func2`, which generate pure functions for properties over callbacks |
| Anything | `Any`, a bounded mix of common types, and `Make[T]`, which derives a generator from a type (chapter 9) |

Integers lean toward the boundaries of their range and toward small values, because those are where bugs live. Lengths of strings and collections follow the size parameter of the case. A maximum length of `-1` means no bound. Strings in the formats that standards define, such as RFC 3339 timestamps, e-mail addresses and URIs, come from the package `go.ymotongpoo.com/pbt/format`, which chapter 10 describes.

## Times and addresses

The generators of times and addresses follow the same rule as the integers: they lean toward the values where code breaks. `Time` draws an instant between the zero `time.Time` and the end of year 9999. It moves nearly half of the instants to an edge of the calendar: the first or last nanosecond of a day, a month or a year, February 29, or a bound of the range. In a share of the cases, it also rounds the fraction of a second to whole microseconds, milliseconds or seconds, since stored timestamps mostly carry those. A date one month ahead is a classic victim.

```go
var billingProperty = func(t *pbt.T) {
	start := pbt.Time().Draw(t, "")
	next := nextBillingDate(start)
	if want := (start.Month() % 12) + 1; next.Month() != want {
		t.Fatalf("next billing date %s is not in %s", next.Format(time.DateOnly), want)
	}
}
```

```text
[pbt] property failed after 39 passed checks and 13 shrink steps (size 40)
[pbt] start (Time()) = time.Date(1970, time.January, 31, 23, 59, 59, 999999999, time.UTC)
[pbt] error: next billing date 1970-03-03 is not in February
[pbt] reproduce: go test -run 'TestBilling' -pbt.seed=0x1
```

`AddDate` normalizes January 31 plus one month to March 3. The run found the last nanosecond of a month. The shrinker then moved it to January 1970, the month of the Unix epoch, which is where `Time` shrinks. `TimeRange(lo, hi)` keeps values in a range and in the location of `lo`. In a location with daylight saving time, it also moves values next to a change of offset: to the moment of the change, the nanosecond before it, or the half hours around it. `Zone` loads IANA time zones, by default a list of zones with unusual rules, and `FixedZone` draws fixed offsets.

The address generators return the types of `net/netip`. `IPv4` and `IPv6` draw a share of their addresses from the special-purpose blocks of RFC 6890. Among them are loopback, private networks, link local, documentation and multicast, and, for IPv6, IPv4-mapped addresses. `AddrIn` keeps addresses inside the prefixes you give it.

```go
// The client of a request is an address inside the private networks of
// RFC 1918, and the rate limiter keys clients by their /24.
func TestClientKey(t *testing.T) {
	private := pbt.AddrIn(
		netip.MustParsePrefix("10.0.0.0/8"),
		netip.MustParsePrefix("172.16.0.0/12"),
		netip.MustParsePrefix("192.168.0.0/16"),
	)
	pbt.Check(t, func(t *pbt.T) {
		client := private.Draw(t, "client")
		key := netip.PrefixFrom(client, 24).Masked()
		if !key.Contains(client) || !key.Addr().IsPrivate() {
			t.Fatalf("key %s does not cover %s", key, client)
		}
	})
}
```

## Strings that match a pattern

`StringMatching` builds strings from a regular expression in the syntax of package `regexp`. Every value matches the whole pattern, and shrinking keeps it matching. Alternations shrink toward earlier branches, repetitions toward their minimum count, and character classes toward their first printable ASCII member. `RuneIn` draws runes from the range tables of package `unicode`, such as scripts and categories. Every range of the tables gets the same chance, so a small script is not drowned out by the CJK ideographs.

```go
// An order number has two capital letters, a dash and four digits.
var orderID = regexp.MustCompile(`^[A-Z]{2}-\d{4}$`)

func TestOrderIDs(t *testing.T) {
	pbt.Check(t, func(t *pbt.T) {
		id := pbt.StringMatching(`[A-Z]{2}-\d{4}`).Draw(t, "id")
		if !orderID.MatchString(id) {
			t.Fatalf("%q is not an order number", id)
		}
		name := pbt.StringOfN(pbt.RuneIn(unicode.Hiragana, unicode.Katakana, unicode.Han), 1, 8).Draw(t, "name")
		if label := fmt.Sprintf("%s %s", id, name); len([]rune(label)) > 16 {
			t.Fatalf("label %q is too long", label)
		}
	})
}
```

## Building your own

`pbt.Custom` turns a function of `*pbt.T` into a generator. Inside it you draw from other generators, in any order and under any control flow.

```go
type User struct {
	Name  string
	Age   int
	Email string
}

// userGen builds a User from smaller generators. Labeled draws inside a
// generator appear in the report, indented under the value they build.
var userGen = pbt.Custom("user", func(t *pbt.T) User {
	name := pbt.StringOfN(pbt.SampledFrom([]rune("abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz")), 1, 12).Draw(t, "name")
	return User{
		Name:  name,
		Age:   pbt.IntRange(0, 120).Draw(t, "age"),
		Email: name + "@example.com",
	}
})
```

The name given to `Custom` is how the generator appears in reports. The labels of the draws inside it matter too: a labeled draw inside a generator is listed in the report, indented under the value it helped to build. Unlabeled draws, with `""`, are not listed, which is right for a value that is not interesting on its own.

## Composing generators

Three functions cover most compositions.

```go
// Map transforms a value, Filter keeps the values that satisfy a predicate,
// and Bind picks the next generator from a value.
var (
	even    = pbt.Map(pbt.IntRange(0, 500), func(n int) int { return 2 * n })
	nonZero = pbt.Filter(pbt.Int(), func(n int) bool { return n != 0 })
	matrix  = pbt.Bind(pbt.IntRange(1, 4), func(n int) pbt.Gen[[][]int] {
		row := pbt.SliceOfN(pbt.Int(), n, n) // every row has the same length
		return pbt.SliceOfN(row, 1, 4)
	})
)
```

- `Map` applies a function to each value. The result shrinks as the input does.
- `Filter` discards the values that fail a predicate and draws again. A predicate that rejects most values makes the run slow, and pbt gives up on a case after many rejections. Prefer building the value you want: `IntRange(1, 100)` over `Filter(Int(), positive)`.
- `Bind` chooses the next generator from a value, which is how one part of a value can depend on another. PropEr calls it `?LET`.

`OneOf` picks one of several generators with equal probability and `Frequency` with weights; chapter 2 covers them. `Ptr` wraps a value in a pointer, with or without `nil`. `Lazy` defers the construction of a generator until it is first drawn from, which is what a recursive generator needs to refer to itself; chapter 9 shows the bounded form.

## Reports show how a value was built

A property that fails on a `User` reports the user and, under it, the labeled parts.

```go
var displayNameProperty = func(t *pbt.T) {
	u := userGen.Draw(t, "user")
	display := strings.ToUpper(u.Name[:1]) + u.Name[1:]
	if unicode.IsLower(rune(display[0])) {
		t.Fatalf("display name %q is not capitalized", display)
	}
	if len(display) > 8 {
		t.Fatalf("display name %q is too long for the badge", display)
	}
}
```

```text
[pbt] property failed after 3 passed checks and 189 shrink steps (size 4)
[pbt] user (user) = snippets.User{Name:"aaaaaaaaa", Age:0, Email:"aaaaaaaaa@example.com"}
[pbt]   name (StringOfN(SampledFrom(26 values), 1, 12)) = "aaaaaaaaa"
[pbt]   age (IntRange(0, 120)) = 0
[pbt] error: display name "Aaaaaaaaa" is too long for the badge
[pbt] reproduce: go test -run 'TestDisplayName' -pbt.seed=0x1
```

The name shrank to the shortest string that still breaks the length check, nine letters of `a`, and the age to 0 because it played no part in the failure. A report lists labeled draws up to three levels deep and cuts each value at 2000 characters; the `ReportDepth` and `ReportLimit` options change both.

A draw at the top level of the property appears in the report even without a label. When the draw is assigned to a single variable, as in `start := pbt.Time().Draw(t, "")` above, the report names the value after the variable. Otherwise it gives the file and the line of the draw, as in `Int() at prop_test.go:12 = 5`. The report reads the source file to find the variable. When the file is not available, for example in a binary built with `-trimpath`, the report gives the line. `Verbose()` or `-pbt.v` adds the line to every draw.

## Sampling outside a property

`Example` returns one value of a generator, for a quick look or for a conventional test that needs a plausible input. A seed makes the value stable for the same generator code and pbt version.

```go
func TestExample(t *testing.T) {
	u := userGen.Example(42) // a sample outside any property; the seed fixes it
	if u.Age < 0 || !strings.HasSuffix(u.Email, "@example.com") {
		t.Fatalf("unexpected user %+v", u)
	}
}
```

## Values that generators share

`Just(v)` returns the same `v` for every case. When `v` is a slice, a map or a pointer, every case sees the same object, so a property that modifies it changes what later cases and the report see. `SampledFrom(values)` copies the slice but hands out the elements as they are. Draw a fresh value from `Custom` when the property needs to modify it.

---

# Size, distribution and statistics

pbt lets you decide what the data looks like, and gives you the tools to check that it looks the way you intended. Both halves matter: a property that never reaches the interesting states of a system proves nothing about them.

## The size parameter

Every test case runs at a size. `Check` starts at size 1 and raises it by one for each passing case, up to 42, so a run begins with small inputs and ends with large ones. The lengths of strings, slices and maps average the size; the magnitude of integers grows with it too. `t.Size()` returns the size of the current case, and the `Sizes(start, max)` option or the `-pbt.startsize` and `-pbt.maxsize` flags change the range.

`Sized` builds a generator from the size, which is how PropEr's `?SIZED` works, and `Resize` runs a generator at a fixed size. Together they bound a recursive structure.

```go
// A tree whose depth follows the size parameter: small early cases, larger
// later ones. Resize fixes the size of a part of a value.
type Tree struct {
	Value    int
	Children []Tree
}

func tree() pbt.Gen[Tree] {
	return pbt.Sized(func(size int) pbt.Gen[Tree] {
		if size <= 1 {
			return pbt.Map(pbt.Int(), func(v int) Tree { return Tree{Value: v} })
		}
		return pbt.Custom("tree", func(t *pbt.T) Tree {
			child := pbt.Resize(size/2, tree())
			return Tree{Value: pbt.Int().Draw(t, ""), Children: pbt.SliceOfN(child, 0, 3).Draw(t, "")}
		})
	})
}
```

Halving the size at every level gives a tree whose depth is at most the logarithm of the size, whatever the branching. For size-sensitive collection generators such as `SliceOf`, `Resize(0, g)` produces an empty collection unless a positive minimum length is required. `Resize` fixes only the size parameter, so the length bounds stated by `SliceOfN` still hold: `Resize(0, SliceOfN(Int(), 1, 3))` gives one element.

## Weights

`Frequency` draws one of its alternatives with a probability proportional to its weight.

```go
type Op struct {
	Kind string
	Key  string
}

// ops reads four times as often as it writes; shrinking moves toward the
// first alternative, the read.
var ops = pbt.Frequency(
	pbt.W(4, pbt.Map(pbt.StringN(1, 3), func(k string) Op { return Op{"get", k} })),
	pbt.W(1, pbt.Map(pbt.StringN(1, 3), func(k string) Op { return Op{"put", k} })),
)
```

Weights only affect generation. Shrinking always moves toward the first alternative, whatever the weights are, so the order of the alternatives is the shrinking priority. An alternative with weight 0 is never generated and is reachable only by shrinking, which is what `ShrinkTo` in chapter 3 is built on. `OneOf` is `Frequency` with equal weights.

## Statistics

Four methods on `*pbt.T` describe the cases of a run. `Check` prints the result when the property passes.

```go
func TestOperationMix(t *testing.T) {
	pbt.Check(t, func(t *pbt.T) {
		batch := pbt.SliceOfN(ops, 1, 20).Draw(t, "batch")
		writes := 0
		for _, op := range batch {
			t.Aggregate(op.Kind) // share of each kind among all operations
			if op.Kind == "put" {
				writes++
			}
		}
		t.Classify(writes == 0, "read-only batch") // share of cases
		t.Measure("batch length", float64(len(batch)))
		t.Cover(writes > 0, 60, "has a write")
	}, pbt.CheckCoverage())
}
```

- `Classify(cond, label)` records a label when the condition holds, and `Collect(v)` records the text of a value as a label. Both report a share of passing cases as long as a case records each label once. They do not remove repeats, so a case that records a label twice counts twice and a share can exceed 100%. Use `Aggregate` for what happens several times in a case. `Cover` counts a case once per label.
- `Aggregate(values...)` counts samples, several per case, and reports their share of all samples. It is the right call for the names of the commands a stateful test ran.
- `Measure(name, value)` records a number and reports its minimum, average and maximum.

```text
[pbt] OK, passed 100 checks (seed 0x1)
[pbt]  22.0% read-only batch
[pbt]  81.1% get
[pbt]  18.9% put
[pbt] batch length: min 1, avg 12.43, max 20 (100 samples)
```

The shares confirm the four-to-one weighting, and the length line confirms that batches of the full length occur. `Verbose()` or `-pbt.v` prints the summary even when the property records nothing.

## Checking coverage

`Cover(cond, pct, label)` turns an observation into a requirement: the cases for which `cond` holds must make up at least `pct` percent of all passing cases. The example above requires a write in 60% of the batches.

For requirements below 100%, the decision is statistical, since a run of 100 cases can miss a 60% share by chance. pbt computes the 99.7% confidence interval of the observed share, the Wilson score interval. The requirement is met when the interval's lower bound reaches `pct`, unmet when its upper bound is below `pct`, and undecided otherwise. A requirement of 100% is not statistical: it is met while every passing case records a hit for the label and unmet as soon as one does not. Without the `CheckCoverage` option, `Check` logs a shortfall and passes. With it, `Check` keeps running cases past the configured number, up to twenty times as many, until every requirement is decided. It then fails on a shortfall, and it also fails when a requirement is still undecided, so a pass means that the data supports the share.

```go
var rareCoverProperty = func(t *pbt.T) {
	n := pbt.IntRange(0, 999).Draw(t, "n")
	t.Cover(n%100 == 0, 30, "round hundred") // too rare for a 30% share
}
```

```text
[pbt] insufficient coverage:
[pbt]   round hundred: 17.6% of 125 cases, required 30.0%
```

The run stopped after 125 cases, once the interval excluded 30%. The observed share also says something about `IntRange`: 0 is a boundary value, so it occurs far more often than one case in a thousand. Statistics are how you find that out, and `Frequency` or `SampledFrom` are how you change it when a uniform spread is what the property needs.

## Health checks

Statistics answer the questions you ask. Health checks answer the ones you might not think of: whether the run spends its cases well. `Check` watches every run and warns about wasted input, expensive generation and changes to saved inputs. An optional check also detects repeated choices.

| Check | Warns when |
| --- | --- |
| `HealthFilter` | half of the cases, and at least 20, are discarded by `Assume`, `Skip` or a `Filter` that gave up; or a `Filter` rejects nine values in ten over at least 100 |
| `HealthLarge` | a fifth of the cases draw more than 10,000 choices |
| `HealthSlow` | drawing the values takes 10 ms per case and a second in all, not counting the property's own work |
| `HealthStale` | a saved case's draw comments differ from the draws produced by replay; warns by default |
| `HealthDuplicate` | fewer than half the inputs have distinct choice sequences over at least 20 non-discarded random cases; off by default |

A property that keeps only long strings shows the first one.

```go
// Most strings that String draws at small sizes are shorter than eight
// runes, so Assume throws most cases away.
var longNameProperty = func(t *pbt.T) {
	name := pbt.String().Draw(t, "name")
	t.Assume(len([]rune(name)) >= 8)
	if short := []rune(name)[:8]; len(short) != 8 {
		t.Fatalf("prefix %q", string(short))
	}
}
```

```text
[pbt] health: HealthFilter: 629 of 729 cases were discarded; most by Assume at health_test.go:18 (629) (CheckHealth(HealthFilter) makes this fail; IgnoreHealth(HealthFilter) hides it)
```

The run passed, but it ran 729 cases to get its 100, and the warning names the line that threw the rest away. A generator that builds long strings, `StringN(8, 40)`, removes the waste. The warning names the busiest sources: the description of a `Filter`, or the line of an `Assume` or a `Skip`. `HealthLarge` names the draws that consumed the most choices.

All health checks except `HealthDuplicate` warn by default, the way `Cover` does, and the run passes. `CheckHealth()` makes `HealthFilter` and `HealthLarge` fail a passing run. `CheckHealth(HealthSlow)` adds the timing check, which is left out by default because a loaded CI machine can trip it. `CheckHealth(HealthStale)` makes stale replay fail a passing run; `CheckHealth()` leaves it as a warning because generators can change intentionally. `IgnoreHealth(checks...)` hides a check and wins over both `CheckHealth` and `WarnHealth`.

The flags `-pbt.checkhealth` and `-pbt.ignorehealth` take the same names for every `Check` of a `go test` run, for example `-pbt.checkhealth=default,slow`. Two more checks, `HealthFlaky` and `HealthShrink`, apply to failing runs; chapter 3 describes them.

`HealthStale` means that the same saved choices now describe different draw text. It does not mean that a fixed bug still fails. The warning identifies the file and the first changed draw. [Chapter 4](04-properties.md#seeds-saved-cases-and-replay) explains what to inspect before trusting the replay.

`WarnHealth(HealthDuplicate)` or `-pbt.warnhealth=duplicate` enables the duplicate warning. `CheckHealth(HealthDuplicate)` enables it as an error. `WarnHealth()` with no arguments changes nothing. Health flags and options add up; `WarnHealth` cannot downgrade a check that `CheckHealth` makes an error.

```go
func checkSwitch(tb pbt.TB) {
	pbt.Check(tb, func(t *pbt.T) {
		enabled := pbt.Bool().Draw(t, "enabled")
		t.Classify(enabled, "enabled")
	}, pbt.Seed(1), pbt.Checks(20), pbt.WarnHealth(pbt.HealthDuplicate))
}
```

The Boolean domain has only two values. This run intentionally repeats them:

```text
[pbt] health: HealthDuplicate: only 2 of 20 generated inputs were distinct by their choices; possible causes include a small domain such as Bool or SampledFrom, a low maximum size, or more Checks than the input space has values (CheckHealth(HealthDuplicate) makes this fail; IgnoreHealth(HealthDuplicate) hides it)
```

`HealthDuplicate` counts passing and failing cases from ordinary random generation. It excludes discards, saved-case replay, shrinking and targeted search. Coverage-guided mutations also do not count. The key hashes the consumed choices, without the size. Sizes grow during a run, so including size would hide repeated choices in most early cases.

This count is a proxy for distinct values. Different choices can map to the same value, and values derived only from size can count as duplicates. Tracking stops after more than 4096 distinct keys. A small domain can be intentional, which is why this check needs an explicit option.

---

# Shrinking

When a case fails, pbt looks for a simpler case that fails in the same way, and reports that one. The search is automatic for every generator, including the ones you write with `Custom`, `Map` and `Bind`. This chapter explains what "simpler" means, how to steer the search, and what it will not do.

## How a case shrinks

Every value a property draws is a function of a sequence of choices, and pbt records that sequence for each case. The shrinker edits the sequence: it deletes the choices that belong to one draw, lowers numbers, moves a group of choices toward an earlier alternative, reorders elements, and then regenerates the values from the edited sequence. A candidate replaces the current case when the property still fails and the sequence is shorter, or as long and lexicographically smaller. The shrinker also lowers the choice that picks an alternative, and a length that a generator draws before its elements. The new value can then take fewer choices than the old one. The shrinker reconnects the choices that followed the old value, so the draws after it keep their values. The passes repeat until none of them makes progress or the shrink time, 30 seconds by default, runs out.

Because the shrinker works on choices and not on values, nothing special is needed for a value built by `Map` or `Bind`: the shrinker edits the choices underneath and the function regenerates the value. The direction of the search follows from what each generator does with small choices.

| Generator | Shrinks toward |
| --- | --- |
| `Int`, `Float64` and the other numbers | 0, or the bound of the range nearest to 0 |
| `IntRangeToward(lo, hi, center)` | `center`, from either side |
| `Bool` | `false` |
| `String`, `SliceOf`, `MapOf` | fewer elements, then simpler elements |
| `SampledFrom`, `OneOf`, `Frequency` | the first value or alternative, when it takes no more choices than the current one |
| `Just` | nothing to shrink |
| `Custom`, `Map`, `Bind` | whatever the draws inside shrink toward |

## Writing generators that shrink well

The shrinker edits a span of choices as a unit: the choices of one draw, with the draws nested in it. Two habits keep the spans useful.

- Write an alternative as a generator that draws the whole branch, and choose between such generators with `OneOf` or `Frequency`. Avoid drawing an index first and then a `switch` on it. That puts the branch's choices outside the span of the index, and switching the branch disturbs the draws that follow.
- Draw a length first and the elements after it, inside one `Custom`. Lowering the length then removes the last elements and keeps what follows the generator.

```go
// Each alternative draws its whole value, so the choice of the alternative
// and the choices of its value sit in one span, and the shrinker can switch
// from the phone number to the shorter e-mail address without disturbing
// the draws that follow.
var contact = pbt.OneOf(
	pbt.Custom("email", func(t *pbt.T) string {
		return pbt.SampledFrom([]string{"alice", "bob", "carol"}).Draw(t, "") + "@example.com"
	}),
	pbt.Custom("phone", func(t *pbt.T) string {
		return fmt.Sprintf("+81-%d-%04d", pbt.IntRange(10, 99).Draw(t, ""), pbt.IntRange(0, 9999).Draw(t, ""))
	}),
)

var contactProperty = func(t *pbt.T) {
	c := contact.Draw(t, "contact")
	retries := pbt.IntRange(0, 10).Draw(t, "retries")
	if retries > 3 && !strings.Contains(c, "+81-99") {
		t.Fatalf("gave up after %d retries for %s", retries, c)
	}
}
```

From every seed, the report shows `alice@example.com` and 4 retries, whichever contact the failing case had at first. An alternative wins only when it takes no more choices than the current one. Here the e-mail address takes one choice and the phone number two. A first alternative that draws more than the others can stay out of reach. The case then shrinks within the alternative it started from.

## Steering the search

Sometimes the simplest value by that table is not the most readable one. A date is easier to think about in 1970 than in the year 0, and an offset of a few minutes is more telling than one of 720. Two generators change the target.

```go
// year shrinks toward the 1970s, then the 20th century, rather than toward
// the year 0: the alternatives are tried in order while shrinking and never
// used while generating.
var year = pbt.ShrinkTo(pbt.IntRange(0, 9999), pbt.IntRange(1970, 1979), pbt.IntRange(1900, 1999))

// offset shrinks toward 0 from either side instead of toward -720.
var offset = pbt.IntRangeToward(-720, 840, 0)
```

`ShrinkTo(g, alts...)` generates from `g` and, when shrinking, tries the alternatives in order. It is the equivalent of PropEr's `?SHRINK`. A property that fails for every year from 1990 on reports 1990, the lowest failing year inside the first alternative that still fails:

```text
[pbt] year (ShrinkTo(IntRange(0, 9999))) = 1990
```

`IntRangeToward` makes a range shrink toward a center instead of its lower bound. A property that fails outside ±30 minutes reports 31 or -31.

## Shrinking a composite to one of its parts

A value built from parts normally keeps its shape while the parts shrink: a concatenation of three slices stays a concatenation of three slices. `LetShrink` records one more choice, whether to combine the parts or to return one of them. Generation always combines; shrinking can flip the choice, so the composite shrinks to a single part. PropEr calls this `?LETSHRINK`.

```go
// A concatenation that can shrink to one of its parts, as PropEr's
// ?LETSHRINK does; without it, the shrinker could only shorten each part.
var part = pbt.SliceOf(pbt.IntRange(1, 9))

var concat = pbt.LetShrink([]pbt.Gen[[]int]{part, part, part}, func(parts [][]int) []int {
	return slices.Concat(parts...)
})
```

A property that fails on two or more elements reports `[]int{1, 1}`, with the other two parts gone.

## Keeping a value as it is

`NoShrink` marks a value that the shrinker must leave alone. Use it for opaque tokens and for inputs whose shape is fixed by the system under test, where shrinking would only spend time.

A collection can still drop an element generated with `NoShrink`; the elements that remain keep their values.

```go
// A token the system under test treats as opaque; shrinking it would only
// slow the search down.
var token = pbt.NoShrink(pbt.StringOfN(pbt.SampledFrom([]rune("0123456789abcdef")), 32, 32))
```

## Watching a shrink

`SampleShrink` returns the path a value takes when it shrinks, as PropEr's `sampleshrink` does. It is the quickest way to check that a custom generator shrinks toward what you expect.

```go
func TestSampleShrink(t *testing.T) {
	var path []int
	for xs := range pbt.SampleShrink(pbt.SliceOfN(pbt.IntRange(1, 9), 1, 5), 1) {
		path = append(path, len(xs))
	}
	if path[len(path)-1] != 1 {
		t.Fatalf("the shrink path ended at length %d", path[len(path)-1])
	}
}
```

In a real run, `Verbose()` or `-pbt.v` logs every accepted shrink step with the values it produced.

## The failure stays the same

A case records how it first failed: the line of the assertion, or the type and location of the panic. During shrinking, a candidate is accepted only when it fails in the same way. The rule protects you from a common trap.

```go
// Two bugs: a panic for large inputs and a wrong answer for the rest. The
// shrinker keeps the failure it started from, so a panic found at a large
// input is reported as a panic, at the smallest input that still panics.
func lookupDiscount(qty int) int {
	if qty > 1000 {
		panic("quantity out of range")
	}
	if qty > 100 {
		return 5
	}
	return 0
}

var discountProperty = func(t *pbt.T) {
	qty := pbt.IntRange(0, 5000).Draw(t, "qty")
	if d := lookupDiscount(qty); qty > 100 && d != 10 {
		t.Fatalf("discount for %d units = %d, want 10", qty, d)
	}
}
```

Suppose the first failing case is a quantity of 3000, which panics. Without the rule, the shrinker would lower the quantity past 1000, find that 101 fails the assertion, and report a wrong discount; the panic would be gone from the report. With the rule, the quantity shrinks to 1001 and the report shows the panic. When the first failure is the wrong discount, the case shrinks to 101 instead. Either way, the report describes the bug the run found. A stateful test keys its failures by command and check, so a failing postcondition of one command cannot turn into the panic of another.

One assertion site can cover several causes. `t.Signature(name)` assigns a stable name to the cause for the current case. This version of the [port property in chapter 4](04-properties.md#several-failures-in-one-run) uses one `Fatalf` for both bugs:

```go
// parsePort is the parser with two bugs from chapter 4.
var namedPortProperty = func(t *pbt.T) {
	s := pbt.StringOf(pbt.SampledFrom([]rune("0123456789"))).Draw(t, "s")
	_, accepted := parsePort(s)
	want := validPort(s)
	if accepted != want {
		cause := "rejected valid port"
		if accepted {
			cause = "accepted invalid port"
		}
		t.Signature(cause)
		t.Fatalf("parsePort(%q): %s", s, cause)
	}
}
```

Running it with `Seed(1)` and `MaxFailures(2)` produces:

```text
[pbt] failure 1 of 2: property failed after 6 passed checks and 9 shrink steps (size 4)
[pbt] failure was named "accepted invalid port"
[pbt] s (StringOf(SampledFrom(10 values))) = "0"
[pbt] error: parsePort("0"): accepted invalid port
[pbt] reproduce: go test -run 'TestNamedPort' -pbt.seed=0x1 -pbt.failures=2
[pbt] failure 2 of 2: property failed after 6 passed checks and 90 shrink steps (size 8)
[pbt] failure was named "rejected valid port"
[pbt] s (StringOf(SampledFrom(10 values))) = "7000"
[pbt] error: parsePort("7000"): rejected valid port
[pbt] reproduce: go test -run 'TestNamedPort' -pbt.seed=0x1 -pbt.failures=2
```

The name replaces the assertion site, panic type and site, or stateful command check as the failure identity. Shrinking keeps that name, and `MaxFailures` counts different names as different failures. The same identity determines saved-file suffixes when collecting several failures and the replay comparison for `HealthFlaky`.

Choose names for causes, without generated values. Otherwise each value can become a separate failure and prevent shrinking. Without `Signature`, the automatic identity still applies. A call before or after a failure works; the last call wins, including deferred calls and cleanup callbacks. `Conjunction` shares one case, so a signature in any member names the whole case. A passing case ignores the name.

## When a failure does not recur

Before shrinking, `Check` replays the failing case once with the same choices. A property that depends only on its input fails again, in the same way. The replay can pass, discard the case or fail at another place. Then the property or a generator depends on something besides the choices, such as a clock, a global variable or the order of goroutines. The report then carries a `HealthFlaky` note.

```go
// The cache keeps a hit counter across cases, so the outcome of a case
// depends on the cases that ran before it.
var hits atomic.Int64

var flakyProperty = func(t *pbt.T) {
	key := pbt.IntRange(0, 9).Draw(t, "key")
	if hits.Add(1)%7 == 0 && key > 2 {
		t.Fatalf("cache miss for key %d", key)
	}
}
```

```text
[pbt] property failed after 55 passed checks and 3 shrink steps (size 42)
[pbt] key (IntRange(0, 9)) = 4
[pbt] error: cache miss for key 4
[pbt] reproduce: go test -run 'TestCache' -pbt.seed=0x1
[pbt] health: HealthFlaky: the failure did not recur when its input was replayed (the replay passed); the original failure was at flaky_test.go:21 (IgnoreHealth(HealthFlaky) hides it)
```

`Check` still shrinks and saves the case, since a failure that recurs only sometimes, such as a race in chapter 6, is still a failure. The note tells you that the shrunk case may not fail again when you replay it. Fix the property before you trust its reports. A parallel test of chapter 6 that catches a race can carry the note, and there it is expected.

## What shrinking will not do

The shrinker reaches a local minimum, not always the global one: it only accepts candidates that are simpler by its own measure, so a smaller case that needs a larger intermediate step stays out of reach. `LetShrink` and `ShrinkTo` exist for the cases where the structure of a value hides the simpler form. The size parameter stays fixed while a case shrinks, and the time budget is 30 seconds per failure; `ShrinkTime` or `-pbt.shrinktime` change it. Shrinking can stop at the budget or at its fixed limit of 200,000 steps. The report then carries a `HealthShrink` note, because a smaller case may exist.

---

# Properties and runs

This chapter covers the shape of a run: how many cases, which sizes, how discards are handled, what runs before and after a case, how properties combine, and how a failure is reproduced.

## Options and flags

Most settings have a flag for the whole `go test` run and an option for one `Check` call. Options win over flags, except for the health checks, where the flags and the options add up.

| Flag | Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-pbt.checks` | `Checks(n)` | 100 | passing cases required |
| `-pbt.seed` | `Seed(s)` | random | seed of the run, printed in every report |
| `-pbt.startsize`, `-pbt.maxsize` | `Sizes(start, max)` | 1, 42 | size of the first case and the size the cases grow to |
| `-pbt.budget` | `Budget(d)` | 0 (unlimited) | elapsed time allowed for search, excluding replay and shrinking |
| `-pbt.shrinktime` | `ShrinkTime(d)` | 30s | time budget for shrinking one failure |
| `-pbt.failures` | `MaxFailures(n)` | 1 | distinct failures to collect, shrink and report |
| `-pbt.causality` | `Causality(n)` | 0 (off) | continuations per prefix to locate a possible cause in a sequential program (chapter 5) |
| `-pbt.coverage` | `CoverageGuided()` | false | use live block coverage to guide search (chapter 8) |
| `-pbt.json` | `ReportJSON(path)` | empty (off) | append one JSON report per run |
| `-pbt.observe` | `Observations(dir)` | empty (off) | append OpenPBTStats records, one file per test |
| `-pbt.searchsteps` | `SearchSteps(n)` | 1000 | cases of a targeted search |
| `-pbt.nosave` | `NoSave()` | false | do not save failing cases |
| `-pbt.replay` | `ReplayFile(path)` | none | a saved case to replay before searching |
| `-pbt.v` | `Verbose()` | false | log the summary of a passing run and every shrink step |
| | `TestdataDir(dir)` | `testdata/pbt` | where failing cases are saved |
| | `NoReplay()` | false | skip the saved cases |
| | `Setup(f)` | none | run `f` before every case |
| | `CheckCoverage()` | false | fail on an unmet or undecided `Cover` requirement |
| `-pbt.warnhealth` | `WarnHealth(checks...)` | none | enable optional health warnings, currently `HealthDuplicate` |
| `-pbt.checkhealth` | `CheckHealth(checks...)` | none | health checks that fail a passing run (chapter 2) |
| `-pbt.ignorehealth` | `IgnoreHealth(checks...)` | none | health checks to hide |
| | `ReportLimit(chars)`, `ReportDepth(levels)` | 2000, 3 | size of a reported value and depth of nested draws |

```go
func TestSortIsIdempotent(t *testing.T) {
	pbt.Check(t, func(t *pbt.T) {
		xs := pbt.SliceOf(pbt.Int()).Draw(t, "xs")
		once := slices.Sorted(slices.Values(xs))
		twice := slices.Sorted(slices.Values(once))
		if !slices.Equal(once, twice) {
			t.Fatalf("sorting twice gave %v, then %v", once, twice)
		}
	}, pbt.Checks(500), pbt.Sizes(1, 60))
}

// MakeCheck turns a property into a test function, for table-driven or
// generated tests.
var TestReverseTwice = pbt.MakeCheck(func(t *pbt.T) {
	xs := pbt.SliceOf(pbt.Rune()).Draw(t, "xs")
	ys := slices.Clone(xs)
	slices.Reverse(ys)
	slices.Reverse(ys)
	if !slices.Equal(xs, ys) {
		t.Fatalf("reversing twice changed %v", xs)
	}
})
```

`MakeCheck` wraps a property as a `func(*testing.T)`, which is convenient for a table of properties or for a subtest.

## Time budgets

`Budget(d)` or `-pbt.budget=d` limits the elapsed search time. The default, zero, leaves search unlimited by time. The clock starts after saved-case replay. pbt checks it before each new case, including discarded cases, targeted search steps and extended `CheckCoverage` runs.

The case limit still applies, so `Budget` does not promise a minimum runtime. Raise `Checks` to run for roughly the requested duration. For a property that calls `Maximize` or `Minimize`, raise `SearchSteps` instead.

```sh
go test -count=1 -run '^TestQueue$' -pbt.checks=1000000 -pbt.budget=30s
```

A running case finishes before the budget takes effect. Use `go test -timeout` for a property that can hang. Replay and shrinking fall outside this budget; `ShrinkTime` separately bounds shrinking each failure or witness.

A `Check` can pass with fewer than `Checks` cases when time runs out. Collected failures still fail, shrink and appear in the report. Enabled health checks and `CheckCoverage` can also fail the run; an undecided coverage requirement remains a failure. `CheckExists` fails if it finds no witness.

A passing run that exhausts its budget always prints a summary, even without `Verbose`. `TestSearchBudget` uses `testing/synctest` to run three one-second cases without a real wait:

```text
[pbt] OK, passed 3 checks in the 3s budget (seed 0x1)
```

## Discarding cases

`t.Assume(cond)` discards the current case when the condition is false, as PropEr's `?IMPLIES` does. A discarded case counts neither as a pass nor as a failure, and `Check` draws another. `Skip`, `Skipf` and `SkipNow` do the same. A failure already recorded in the case takes precedence over a later discard.

```go
func TestDivision(t *testing.T) {
	pbt.Check(t, func(t *pbt.T) {
		a := pbt.Int().Draw(t, "a")
		b := pbt.Int().Draw(t, "b")
		t.Assume(b != 0) // discards the case; too many discards fail the run
		if (a/b)*b+a%b != a {
			t.Fatalf("division identity fails for %d / %d", a, b)
		}
	})
}
```

Discards are a budget. When they exceed ten times the number of checks, the run fails with the reason of the last discard, because a property that discards most of its cases is testing less than it claims. Prefer a generator that produces valid input, `IntMin(1)` over `Assume(b > 0)`, whenever one exists.

## Setup and cleanup

The `Setup` option runs a function before every case. It may return a teardown function, which runs after the case. `t.Cleanup` registers a function from inside the property for the same purpose, and the cleanups run in reverse order after the case, failed or not.

Every cleanup runs even if another cleanup panics or discards. A cleanup failure fails the case even if the property discarded it; a cleanup discard cannot erase a failure or panic from the property. If both the property and a cleanup panic, the report keeps the property's panic.

```go
func TestFileRoundTrip(t *testing.T) {
	dir := t.TempDir()
	withFile := pbt.Setup(func(t *pbt.T) func() {
		path := filepath.Join(dir, "case")
		t.Cleanup(func() { os.Remove(path) }) // Cleanup runs after the case, latest first
		return nil                            // or return a teardown function
	})
	pbt.Check(t, func(t *pbt.T) {
		data := pbt.Bytes().Draw(t, "data")
		path := filepath.Join(dir, "case")
		if err := os.WriteFile(path, data, 0o644); err != nil {
			t.Fatal(err)
		}
		got, err := os.ReadFile(path)
		if err != nil || !slices.Equal(got, data) {
			t.Fatalf("read back %v (%v), want %v", got, err, data)
		}
	}, withFile)
}
```

## Combining properties

`Conjunction` runs several named properties on the same case and names the ones that fail. A later sub-property that discards the case does not erase an earlier sub-property's failure. `Deadline` fails a case that takes longer than a duration.

```go
func TestStringProperties(t *testing.T) {
	// Conjunction runs every sub-property on the same case and names the
	// ones that fail.
	pbt.Check(t, pbt.Conjunction(
		pbt.Named{Name: "upper is idempotent", Prop: func(t *pbt.T) {
			s := pbt.String().Draw(t, "s")
			if strings.ToUpper(strings.ToUpper(s)) != strings.ToUpper(s) {
				t.Fatalf("%q", s)
			}
		}},
		pbt.Named{Name: "fields never contain spaces", Prop: func(t *pbt.T) {
			s := pbt.String().Draw(t, "s")
			for _, f := range strings.Fields(s) {
				if strings.ContainsRune(f, ' ') {
					t.Fatalf("%q", f)
				}
			}
		}},
	))

	// Deadline fails a case that takes too long. Go cannot stop a running
	// function, so the check happens after the property returns.
	pbt.Check(t, pbt.Deadline(time.Second, func(t *pbt.T) {
		s := pbt.StringN(0, 100).Draw(t, "s")
		if strings.Repeat(s, 2) != s+s {
			t.Fatal("repeat")
		}
	}))
}
```

A failure of a conjunction names its members:

```text
[pbt] error: non-empty: empty
[pbt] error: conjunction: [non-empty] failed
```

Go cannot interrupt a running function, so `Deadline` checks the elapsed time after the property returns. A property that never returns is caught by `go test -timeout`. `Timeout` is the former name of `Deadline` and still works.

## Explaining a failure

`t.OnFail(f)` registers a function that runs only for the case that is reported, after shrinking. Anything it logs appears in the report, which makes it the place to print the state of the system under test or the intermediate values of a computation, as PropEr's `?WHENFAIL` does.

```go
func TestOnFail(t *testing.T) {
	pbt.Check(t, func(t *pbt.T) {
		xs := pbt.SliceOf(pbt.Int()).Draw(t, "xs")
		sum := 0
		t.OnFail(func() { t.Logf("partial sum when it failed: %d", sum) }) // runs only for the reported case
		for _, x := range xs {
			sum += x
		}
		if len(xs) == 0 && sum != 0 {
			t.Fatal("impossible")
		}
	})
}
```

## Panics

A panic inside a property fails the case. The report shows the panic value and the frames of your code, and the shrinker looks for the smallest case that panics at the same place. Two helpers cover the properties that are about panics themselves.

```go
func mustPositive(n int) int {
	if n <= 0 {
		panic("not positive")
	}
	return n
}

func TestPanics(t *testing.T) {
	// Recover turns a panic into a value for a property to assert on.
	pbt.Check(t, func(t *pbt.T) {
		n := pbt.IntMax(0).Draw(t, "n")
		if p := pbt.Recover(func() { mustPositive(n) }); p == nil {
			t.Fatalf("mustPositive(%d) did not panic", n)
		}
	})
	// NoPanic generates the arguments of a function from its signature and
	// fails when a call panics.
	pbt.Check(t, pbt.NoPanic(strings.Repeat, pbt.WithType(pbt.IntRange(0, 3))))
}
```

`Recover` runs a function and returns what it panicked with, or nil, so a property can assert that invalid input panics. `NoPanic` takes a function and generates its arguments with `Make`, which chapter 9 describes; the `WithType` and `WithField` options narrow the arguments.

## Several failures in one run

A run normally stops at the first failure, shrinks it and reports it. A function with two bugs then shows them one at a time: you fix the first and run again to meet the second. `MaxFailures(n)` or `-pbt.failures=n` keeps the run going after a failure. It collects up to `n` failures that fail in different ways, shrinks each one, saves each one and reports each one.

```go
var portProperty = func(t *pbt.T) {
	s := pbt.StringOf(pbt.SampledFrom([]rune("0123456789"))).Draw(t, "s")
	n, ok := parsePort(s)
	if ok && !validPort(s) {
		t.Fatalf("parsePort(%q) accepted %d", s, n)
	}
	if !ok && validPort(s) {
		t.Fatalf("parsePort(%q) rejected a valid port", s)
	}
}
```

```text
[pbt] failure 1 of 2: property failed after 6 passed checks and 9 shrink steps (size 4)
[pbt] s (StringOf(SampledFrom(10 values))) = "0"
[pbt] error: parsePort("0") accepted 0
[pbt] reproduce: go test -run 'TestPort' -pbt.seed=0x1 -pbt.failures=2
[pbt] failure 2 of 2: property failed after 6 passed checks and 90 shrink steps (size 8)
[pbt] s (StringOf(SampledFrom(10 values))) = "7000"
[pbt] error: parsePort("7000") rejected a valid port
[pbt] reproduce: go test -run 'TestPort' -pbt.seed=0x1 -pbt.failures=2
```

By default, two failures are different when they fail at different lines, or panic with different types or at different places. That is the same identity that keeps a shrink on one bug (chapter 3). A failure that the shrinker meets on the way, failing in a new way, becomes one of the `n` as well. Each failure gets the full `ShrinkTime` budget. The second minimum, 7000, is a local one. The true boundary is 6554, but the path to it needs a larger digit in a later place, and the shrinker does not try that. Saved failures replay together, and a run that replays a failing saved case does not search for more. `CheckExists` ignores the option.

When several causes share one assertion, call `t.Signature` with a stable name for each cause. `MaxFailures` then collects the names separately, even though every failure reaches the same line. The [named port example in chapter 3](03-shrinking.md#the-failure-stays-the-same) separates an invalid port that the parser accepts from a valid port that it rejects.

## Seeds, saved cases and replay

Every report ends with a `reproduce:` line that carries the seed of the run. Passing that seed with `-pbt.seed` repeats the same sequence of cases, including the failing one, on the same version of both the property code and pbt. Updating pbt can change the generated cases for a seed. In v0.3.2 the integer generation fix changes some seeded runs. In v0.4.0, `Make` generates different values for some recursive types, and the shrinker can reach other, smaller cases. A saved case replays its choices through the generators of the installed version. After an upgrade, a saved case of a property that uses `Make` on a recursive type can produce a different value.

The failing case is also saved under `testdata/pbt/<TestName>/<hash>` as a text file with the size, the drawn values as comments, and the choices. Every later `Check` of the same test replays the saved cases before generating new ones and fails if one still fails, so the regression case follows the code into version control. Keep the file as a regression case after fixing the bug. Removing it drops that replay; do not delete it just to make a run pass. Three options adjust this behavior: `NoSave` keeps a run from writing, `NoReplay` skips the saved cases, and `ReplayFile` or `-pbt.replay=FILE` replays one saved file in any test, which is how you hand a case from one test to another or reproduce a failure from a CI log.

`HealthStale` warns by default when saved draw comments differ from the current replay's draws. A changed generator can turn the same choices into another input. Compare the warning's saved and current text, then test the original value explicitly if it still matters. A passing stale replay does not establish that the original regression is fixed.

The comparison uses rendered text, not deep equality. Truncation can hide changes, and pbt skips draws with unstable representations such as pointers or custom formatters. `CheckHealth(HealthStale)` or `-pbt.checkhealth=stale` makes the warning fail a passing run. `IgnoreHealth(HealthStale)` hides it. Replay does not rewrite the saved comments.

## Machine-readable output

`ReportJSON(path)` or `-pbt.json=path` appends one JSON line after each `Check` or `CheckExists`. The default empty path disables output. Create the parent directory first. The schema name is `go.ymotongpoo.com/pbt/report/v1`; readers should ignore unknown fields.

| Fields | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `test`, `seed`, `kind`, `status`, `errors` | test name, hexadecimal seed, `check` or `exists`, outcome and error messages |
| `checks_passed`, `rejected`, `discards` | search counts, excluding replay and shrinking; `rejected` counts failing candidates |
| `budget_exhausted`, `durations_seconds` | whether time ended the search, plus total, search and shrink durations |
| `failures`, `witness` | failure identities, rendered draws, saved paths and reproduction commands; `witness` appears only after successful `CheckExists` |
| `health`, `statistics`, `objectives` | diagnostics, labels, coverage requirements, measurements and best utilities |

`status` is `passed`, `failed`, `gave_up`, `no_witness` or `error`. Draw values are rendered strings and follow `ReportLimit` and `ReportDepth`. Non-finite numbers use the strings `NaN`, `+Inf` and `-Inf`.

```go
func checkRecordedRun(tb pbt.TB, reportPath, observationDir string) {
	pbt.Check(tb, func(t *pbt.T) {
		n := pbt.IntRange(0, 9).Draw(t, "n")
		t.Classify(n%2 == 0, "even")
		if n < 0 || n > 9 {
			t.Fatalf("out of range: %d", n)
		}
	}, pbt.Seed(1), pbt.Checks(3),
		pbt.ReportJSON(reportPath), pbt.Observations(observationDir))
}
```

`TestMachineReadableOutput` checks both files. This is its JSON report with durations, statistics and empty collections omitted; all shown fields retain their captured values:

```json
{"schema":"go.ymotongpoo.com/pbt/report/v1","test":"TestRecordedRun","seed":"0x1","kind":"check","status":"passed","checks_passed":3,"rejected":0,"discards":0,"budget_exhausted":false}
```

`Observations(dir)` or `-pbt.observe=dir` appends OpenPBTStats records that Tyche reads. The default empty directory disables observations. pbt creates the directory and writes one file per sanitized test name, such as `observations/TestRecordedRun.jsonl`. Subtest names create subdirectories. Sanitized names can collide; `property` and `run_start` distinguish records in a shared file.

Each `test_case` record includes the input, outcome, generation phase, features and timings. Features include labels, measurements, coverage-requirement hits and target utilities. Timings separate input generation from test execution. Replay and shrink attempts also produce records. A `minimal` record with `metadata.final=true` is a snapshot, not another execution. An `info` record ends the run. The `coverage` field is currently null, even with `CoverageGuided`.

```sh
go test -count=1 ./... -pbt.json=runs.jsonl -pbt.observe=observations
```

A log shipper can tail these files and forward records or derived counts to a log or metrics backend. pbt writes files locally and does not send them over the network. Observations use buffering and flush at the end of a run; abrupt termination can lose buffered records. A write error fails the test, because the requested output was not delivered.

---

# Stateful testing

Many bugs only show up after a sequence of operations: a cache that returns a stale value after an eviction, a queue that miscounts after a close. A stateful test describes the operations as commands, keeps a model of what the system should contain, generates sequences of commands against the model, runs them against the real system and checks every result. When a sequence fails, pbt shrinks it to the shortest one that still fails.

## The system under test

The example is a queue that issues ticket numbers and closes them.

```go
// Queue is the system under test: it issues ticket numbers and closes them.
type Queue struct {
	next int
	open map[int]bool
}

func NewQueue() *Queue { return &Queue{open: map[int]bool{}} }

func (q *Queue) Issue() int {
	q.next++
	q.open[q.next] = true
	return q.next
}

var errNotOpen = errors.New("ticket is not open")

func (q *Queue) Close(id int) error {
	if !q.open[id] {
		return errNotOpen
	}
	delete(q.open, id)
	return nil
}

func (q *Queue) Open() int { return len(q.open) }
```

## The model and the commands

The model is what the test believes about the system. Here it is the list of open tickets. The ticket numbers do not exist while the sequence is generated, because nothing has run yet, so the model holds them as `pbt.Var` values, symbolic names for results. PropEr does the same with `{var, N}`.

The model and the system are variables of the property, and the commands are closures over them: nothing is passed around, and no type parameter appears. The property takes a constructor for the queue, so that the same commands run against the correct queue here and against a buggy one below.

```go
// ticketQueue is what the commands need from the system under test.
type ticketQueue interface {
	Issue() int
	Close(id int) error
	Open() int
}

// queueProperty is the stateful property over a queue. The model is what
// the test believes about the queue: the tickets that are open, as Vars,
// because their numbers exist only once Issue has run. The model and the
// queue are variables of the property, and the commands close over them.
func queueProperty(newQueue func() ticketQueue) pbt.Property {
	return func(t *pbt.T) {
		q := newQueue()
		var open []pbt.Var

		issue := pbt.Just(pbt.Command{
			Name: "issue",
			Run:  func(pbt.Env) any { return q.Issue() },
			Next: func(v pbt.Var) { open = append(open, v) },
		})
		closeTicket := func() pbt.CommandGen {
			return pbt.Map(pbt.SampledFrom(open), func(v pbt.Var) pbt.Command {
				return pbt.Command{
					Name: "close", Args: []any{v},
					Pre:  func() bool { return slices.Contains(open, v) },
					Run:  func(env pbt.Env) any { return q.Close(pbt.Resolve[int](env, v)) },
					Next: func(pbt.Var) { open = slices.DeleteFunc(open, func(o pbt.Var) bool { return o == v }) },
					Post: func(_ pbt.Env, got any) error {
						if got != nil {
							return fmt.Errorf("close failed: %v", got)
						}
						return nil
					},
				}
			})
		}
		count := pbt.Just(pbt.Command{
			Name: "open",
			Run:  func(pbt.Env) any { return q.Open() },
			Post: func(_ pbt.Env, got any) error {
				if got != len(open) {
					return fmt.Errorf("%d open tickets, want %d", got, len(open))
				}
				return nil
			},
		})
		// commands chooses the next command from the model: close is only
		// offered while a ticket is open.
		commands := func() pbt.CommandGen {
			if len(open) == 0 {
				return pbt.OneOf(issue, count)
			}
			return pbt.Frequency(pbt.W(3, issue), pbt.W(2, closeTicket()), pbt.W(1, count))
		}
		init := func() { open = nil }

		prog := pbt.Commands(init, commands, pbt.ModelState(func() any { return open })).Draw(t, "cmds")
		prog.RunSequential(t)
	}
}

func TestQueue(t *testing.T) {
	pbt.Check(t, queueProperty(func() ticketQueue { return NewQueue() }))
}
```

A command is a `pbt.Command` value, a struct of functions.

- `Name` and `Args` are what the report prints. Put the arguments of the call in `Args`, with the `Var` of a result where the call uses one, so that the report reads like a program.
- `Pre` says whether the command is allowed in the current state of the model. It is checked whenever a command is generated, and a command that fails it is drawn again. Shrinking also generates commands: removing a command regenerates the ones after it from the new state. If no allowed command is found within the retry limit, the sequence ends, or the case is discarded if its minimum length has not been reached. `RunSequential` checks `Pre` once more before each call; a false result fails the case and usually means that the model was not reset or was changed outside `init` and `Next`.
- `Run` performs the call against the system. The `Env` maps every `Var` to the value its command returned, and `pbt.Resolve[T]` reads one with a type.
- `Next` updates the model for the command. It receives the result as a `Var`, during generation and during execution alike, which keeps the model free of real values and lets the shrinker regenerate the sequence.
- `Post` checks the real result against the model state before the command. It runs during execution only.

`pbt.Commands(init, gen)` is a generator of programs. `init` puts the model in its initial state, and pbt calls it before every generation and every run, so the variables of the model need no copying: `Next` changes them in place, and a replay starts again from `init`. The function `gen` returns the generator of the next command for the current state of the model, which is where you decide what is possible and how likely it is: `close` is only offered while a ticket is open, and a `Frequency` sets the mix, with `pbt.W` pairing each weight with its generator. The type of a command generator is `pbt.CommandGen`, an alias of `pbt.Gen[pbt.Command]`: Go infers the type argument in a call to `Map` or `Frequency` but not in the signature of a function you declare, and the alias is the name to write there. The option `pbt.Length(min, max)` bounds the length of the sequence, a generator that returns `pbt.NoCommands()` ends it, and `pbt.ModelState(f)` gives the report a function that shows the model. `RunSequential` executes the program, checks each postcondition, and records the name of every command for the statistics, so a passing run prints how often each command ran.

## Reading a failure

The next queue forgets to remove a closed ticket, so `Open` keeps counting it.

```go
// leakyQueue forgets to remove a closed ticket, so Open counts it still.
type leakyQueue struct{ Queue }

func (q *leakyQueue) Close(id int) error {
	if !q.open[id] {
		return errNotOpen
	}
	q.open[id] = false
	return nil
}
```

The report shows the program, the history of the run and the model state before the step that failed.

```text
[pbt] property failed after 5 passed checks and 81 shrink steps (size 6)
[pbt] cmds (Commands) = Program{
[pbt]     var1 = issue()
[pbt]     var2 = close(var1)
[pbt]     var3 = open()
[pbt]   }
[pbt] log: history:
[pbt] log:   1. var1 = issue() -> 1
[pbt] log:   2. var2 = close(var1) -> <nil>
[pbt] log:   3. var3 = open() -> 1
[pbt] log: model state before step 3: []
[pbt] error: step 3: postcondition of open() failed: 1 open tickets, want 0
[pbt] reproduce: go test -run 'TestQueue' -pbt.seed=0x1
```

The first failing sequence had several issues and closes. The shrinker removed commands one by one, regenerating the following commands from the new model state and checking their preconditions, until three remained: the shortest program that shows the leak. The failure is keyed by the check and the command, "postcondition of open", so shrinking does not trade it for a different failure.

## Finding the step that caused a failure

The command that detects a failure can run long after the command that caused it. `Causality(n)` or `-pbt.causality=n` samples continuations of the first failing program before shrinking. The default, zero, disables this analysis.

For each sampled prefix, pbt keeps the choices through its last command and generates `n` fresh continuations at the original size. The report gives the fraction that fail with the original failure identity. Discarded continuations do not enter that fraction. A rise suggests that a command in the retained prefix made the failure more likely.

This property loses a value during `write(7)`, then detects the loss in `read()` after four unrelated commands:

```go
var delayedWriteProperty = func(t *pbt.T) {
	step, want, stored := 0, 0, 0
	init := func() { step, want = 0, 0 }
	next := func(pbt.Var) { step++ }
	gen := func() pbt.CommandGen {
		switch step {
		case 0:
			return pbt.Map(pbt.IntRange(0, 15), func(value int) pbt.Command {
				return pbt.Command{
					Name: "write", Args: []any{value},
					Run: func(pbt.Env) any {
						stored = value
						if value == 7 {
							stored = 0 // planted bug: this write loses its value
						}
						return nil
					},
					Next: func(pbt.Var) { want = value; step++ },
				}
			})
		case 5:
			return pbt.Just(pbt.Command{
				Name: "read", Next: next,
				Run: func(pbt.Env) any { return stored },
				Post: func(_ pbt.Env, result any) error {
					if result.(int) != want {
						return fmt.Errorf("read %d, want %d", result, want)
					}
					return nil
				},
			})
		default:
			return pbt.Just(pbt.Command{Name: "wait", Next: next})
		}
	}
	pbt.Commands(init, gen, pbt.Length(6, 6)).Draw(t, "program").RunSequential(t)
}
```

`TestCausalityFindsEarlyWrite` runs it with `Seed(1)` and `Causality(32)`. The report contains these lines; the program, history and later prefix rates are omitted here:

```text
[pbt] property failed after 38 passed checks and 16 shrink steps (size 39)
[pbt] error: step 6: postcondition of read() failed: read 0, want 7
[pbt] reproduce: go test -run 'TestDelayedWrite' -pbt.seed=0x1
[pbt] causality (32 continuations per prefix, seed 0x1):
[pbt]   steps are generated commands of the first failing case, before shrinking in this run
[pbt]   after 0 of 6 steps: 0/32 fail with the same identity
[pbt]   after 1 of 6 steps: 32/32 fail with the same identity <- largest measured rise at step 1: write(7)
```

Keeping the first command makes every sampled continuation fail, although the postcondition fails at step 6. Here `Length(6, 6)` preserves the delayed check during shrinking. In a variable-length program, shrinking can remove commands and change step numbers. The causality report refers to the first failing program before that shrink.

Analysis costs at most `16*n` extra property executions, beyond the usual stability replay. It samples up to eight spaced prefixes and bisects the largest measured rise up to eight times. These executions run setup and cleanup, so reset the system for every property invocation. They do not count toward checks or statistics, call `OnFail`, or save cases.

The analysis applies to sequential `Commands` programs, including `fsm.Commands`. It skips parallel programs because generation order is not execution order. It also skips a failure that the stability replay cannot reproduce. `MaxFailures` analyzes only the first failure; `CheckExists` ignores the option. For a saved case, pbt analyzes the replayed program, since the original unshrunk program is unavailable.

A rise identifies a candidate cause, not proof. Sampling noise can hide a rise, rates can fall again, and a long trace may leave only a range of candidate steps.

## Writing good models

- Change the model only in `init` and `Next`; `Pre`, `Post` and `gen` read it. pbt replays a sequence by calling `init` and then the `Next` of every command, so a change made anywhere else is lost on the replay, and a value that `init` forgets to reset leaks from one case into the next.
- Keep the model simpler than the system. The point is to state what the system should do in terms you can check, not to reimplement it.
- Choose commands from the state rather than rejecting them with `Pre` alone. A precondition that fails often wastes generated commands; a generator that offers the right commands for a state wastes none. Still state the condition in `Pre`. If the generator produces only commands that satisfy it in the current model state, `Pre` rejects nothing during sequential generation, including shrinking. It filters candidates from generators that do not enforce the condition, and `ParallelCommands` uses it to drop commands from branch ends until every interleaving satisfies the preconditions.
- Watch the statistics. `RunSequential` records every command name, so a passing run shows whether the mix of commands is the one you intended.

---

# Parallel testing

A system that is correct under sequential use can still break under concurrent use. pbt tests for that with the same commands and model as a sequential test: it generates a sequential prefix followed by branches, runs the branches in goroutines, and then checks whether some interleaving of the branches explains the results that came back.

```go
// Counter is safe for concurrent use. Add returns the new value, which
// gives the interleaving check a result to explain for every call.
type Counter struct {
	mu sync.Mutex
	n  int
}

func (c *Counter) Add(d int) int {
	c.mu.Lock()
	defer c.mu.Unlock()
	c.n += d
	return c.n
}

func TestCounterParallel(t *testing.T) {
	pbt.Check(t, func(t *pbt.T) {
		c := &Counter{}
		n := 0 // the model: what the counter should hold
		add := pbt.Map(pbt.IntRange(1, 5), func(d int) pbt.Command {
			return pbt.Command{
				Name: "add", Args: []any{d},
				Run:  func(pbt.Env) any { return c.Add(d) },
				Next: func(pbt.Var) { n += d },
				Post: func(_ pbt.Env, got any) error {
					if got != n+d {
						return fmt.Errorf("add(%d) returned %v, want %d", d, got, n+d)
					}
					return nil
				},
			}
		})
		commands := func() pbt.CommandGen { return add }
		prog := pbt.ParallelCommands(func() { n = 0 }, commands).Draw(t, "cmds")
		prog.RunParallel(t)
	})
}
```

`ParallelCommands` takes the same `init` and `gen` as `Commands` and generates programs with two branches of at most six commands each after the prefix. The option `pbt.Branches(n, maxLen)` sets both numbers, with at most three branches and at most twelve commands across them, since the check enumerates interleavings and the count grows fast; `pbt.Length` bounds the prefix. `RunParallel` runs the prefix, then the branches concurrently, and finally searches for an order of the recorded calls and results that satisfies every postcondition in turn. When no order does, the case fails:

```text
[pbt] error: no interleaving of the 2 branches satisfies the postconditions
```

preceded by the program and the history of each branch. A command that panics in a branch fails the case as well.

## What the check means

The check keeps the order of the calls within each branch and tries every order between branches. It accepts the run when one of those orders is consistent with the model. That is what PropEr's `parallel_commands` does, and it is weaker than a linearizability check, which would also respect the real-time order in which calls from different branches completed. A system can pass this check and still violate linearizability in ways only a timing-aware checker sees. It does catch the common failures: lost updates, duplicate identifiers, reads of partial state.

Three consequences follow for how you write the commands.

- The effect of an update must be observable: through its return value, through a later query, or through a separate check after `RunParallel`. A single command may return nothing and leave `Post` nil: that postcondition accepts the result, and pbt uses `Next` to replay the model along candidate orders. Without observations or additional checks, the interleaving check cannot detect a normally returning update that has the wrong effect.
- A branch cannot depend on the results of another branch, since neither has run when the program is generated. Each branch resolves its own `Var` values and those of the prefix.
- The `Run` functions of the branches execute concurrently, so they must not touch the model. `Pre`, `Post` and `Next` run afterwards on the test's goroutine, while pbt replays the model along each candidate order.

## Combine it with the race detector

The interleaving check finds behavior that the model rejects. The race detector finds unsynchronized memory access whether or not it changed a result. Run parallel tests with `go test -race`; the two tools catch different bugs, and a parallel property gives the race detector the concurrent workload it needs.

The `Counter` above holds a mutex. Remove it, and the test reports either duplicated results that no interleaving explains or a data race, depending on the run.

---

# State machines

When a system moves between named states and allows different operations in each, a finite state machine is the natural model. The `fsm` package builds on the command machinery of chapter 5: you name the states and list the transitions out of each one, with weights, and the package generates command sequences that follow the machine. It is the counterpart of PropEr's `proper_fsm`.

## The system

```go
// Account moves between the states new, verified and locked.
type Account struct{ state string }

var errState = errors.New("not allowed in this state")

func (a *Account) Verify() error { return a.move("new", "verified") }
func (a *Account) Lock() error   { return a.move("verified", "locked") }
func (a *Account) Unlock() error { return a.move("locked", "verified") }

func (a *Account) move(from, to string) error {
	if a.state != from {
		return errState
	}
	a.state = to
	return nil
}
```

## The machine

A machine is a function from a state name to the transitions available in that state. `fsm.Commands(initial, init, transitions)` takes the name of the first state, a function that puts the state data in its initial state, and that function. The state data, when a machine has some, lives in variables of the property like the model of chapter 5; `init` may be nil when there is none.

```go
// accountProperty names the states and lists the transitions out of each
// one. The machine carries no state data here; a machine that needs some
// keeps it in variables of the property, like the model of chapter 5.
func accountProperty(t *pbt.T) {
	a := &Account{state: "new"}
	expect := func(want error) func(pbt.Env, any) error {
		return func(_ pbt.Env, got any) error {
			err, _ := got.(error)
			if !errors.Is(err, want) {
				return errors.New("unexpected result")
			}
			return nil
		}
	}
	command := func(name string, call func() error, want error) pbt.CommandGen {
		return pbt.Just(pbt.Command{Name: name, Run: func(pbt.Env) any { return call() }, Post: expect(want)})
	}
	transitions := func(state string) []fsm.Transition {
		switch state {
		case "new":
			return []fsm.Transition{
				{Weight: 3, To: "verified", Cmd: command("verify", a.Verify, nil)},
				{Weight: 1, To: "new", Cmd: command("lock", a.Lock, errState)},
			}
		case "verified":
			return []fsm.Transition{
				{Weight: 2, To: "locked", Cmd: command("lock", a.Lock, nil)},
				{Weight: 1, To: "verified", Cmd: command("verify", a.Verify, errState)},
			}
		default: // locked
			return []fsm.Transition{
				{Weight: 2, To: "verified", Cmd: command("unlock", a.Unlock, nil)},
				{Weight: 1, To: "locked", Cmd: command("lock", a.Lock, errState)},
			}
		}
	}
	prog := fsm.Commands("new", nil, transitions).Draw(t, "cmds")
	prog.RunSequential(t)
}

func TestAccountMachine(t *testing.T) {
	pbt.Check(t, accountProperty)
}
```

Each `Transition` has a `Weight`, a target state `To`, and a `Cmd`, the generator of the command, of type `pbt.CommandGen`. The command's `Pre`, `Next` and `Post` see the state data; the package moves the name. A transition that stays in the same state, like a second `verify` in `verified`, is how a machine tests the operations that must be rejected.

The program runs with `RunSequential` as in chapter 5, and `fsm.ParallelCommands` gives the parallel form of chapter 6. The report shows the state name before the failing step, next to whatever `pbt.ModelState` adds.

## Statistics by state

The commands carry their source and target state, so the summary of a passing run shows which transitions the machine took:

```text
[pbt] OK, passed 100 checks (seed 0x1)
[pbt]  32.7% verified -> locked: lock
[pbt]  31.5% locked -> verified: unlock
[pbt]  17.2% verified -> verified: verify
[pbt]  15.1% locked -> locked: lock
[pbt]   2.8% new -> verified: verify
[pbt]   0.7% new -> new: lock
```

The low share of `new` is expected: every sequence leaves that state after one or two commands and never returns. If a state matters and the statistics show that sequences rarely reach it, raise the weights of the transitions that lead there.

---

# Targeted search and existence

Random inputs reach the common states of a system quickly and the rare ones slowly or never. Targeted property-based testing adds a utility function: the property reports how close a case came to something interesting, and pbt searches for cases with a higher utility instead of drawing fresh ones. PropEr calls it `?MAXIMIZE`.

## Maximize

```go
// A random walk rarely ends far to the right of the origin. Maximize turns
// the run into a search for walks that do, and the property fails once one
// gets past 50; without the search, 100 random cases would almost never
// fail.
var walkProperty = func(t *pbt.T) {
	steps := pbt.SliceOf(pbt.SampledFrom([]int{-1, 1})).Draw(t, "steps")
	pos := 0
	for _, s := range steps {
		pos += s
	}
	t.Maximize("position", float64(pos))
	if pos > 50 {
		t.Fatalf("the walk reached %d", pos)
	}
}
```

A random walk of `n` steps ends about `sqrt(n)` away from the origin, so 100 random walks almost never reach 50. With `t.Maximize("position", pos)`, the run turns into a search once the first case reports a utility. pbt mutates the choices of the best case so far, keeps a mutation when its utility is higher, sometimes keeps a worse one early in the search to escape a local maximum, and occasionally restarts from a fresh case. The search runs for the number of steps set by `SearchSteps` or `-pbt.searchsteps`, 1000 by default, instead of the number of checks.

The report below shortens the list of steps with `…` and omits the reproduction line.

```text
[pbt] property failed after 246 passed checks and 2039 shrink steps (size 33)
[pbt] utility position = 51
[pbt] steps (SliceOf(SampledFrom(2 values))) = []int{1, 1, 1, 1, …}
[pbt] error: the walk reached 51
```

The search found a walk past 50 after 246 cases, and the shrinker then reduced it to 51 steps to the right, the smallest input that fails. When the property passes, the summary reports the best utility seen. `t.Minimize` searches in the other direction. A second `Maximize` with the same name replaces the value of the case.

Use the search when a property has a notion of "closer": the depth of a tree, the length of a queue, the number of retries, the distance to a boundary. A utility that is flat over most inputs gives the search nothing to climb.

## Several objectives

A case can report several utilities under different names. The search then keeps a current and a best case for each objective, and the objectives take turns. Each step mutates the current case of one objective, in the order in which the objectives first appeared. It judges the mutation by that objective's utility alone.

```go
// simulate runs jobs of the given durations on a pool of workers and
// returns the longest queue and the longest wait.
func simulate(jobs []int, workers int) (longestQueue, longestWait int) {
	free := make([]int, workers) // the time at which each worker is free
	for i, d := range jobs {
		w := 0
		for k := range free {
			if free[k] < free[w] {
				w = k
```
