```go
			}
		}
		start := max(free[w], i) // job i arrives at time i
		longestWait = max(longestWait, start-i)
		waiting := 0
		for _, f := range free {
			if f > i {
				waiting++
			}
		}
		longestQueue = max(longestQueue, waiting)
		free[w] = start + d
	}
	return longestQueue, longestWait
}

var poolProperty = func(t *pbt.T) {
	jobs := pbt.SliceOf(pbt.IntRange(1, 10)).Draw(t, "jobs")
	workers := pbt.IntRange(1, 4).Draw(t, "workers")
	queue, wait := simulate(jobs, workers)
	t.Maximize("queue", float64(queue))
	t.Maximize("wait", float64(wait))
	if wait > 100 {
		t.Fatalf("a job waited %d", wait)
	}
}
```

```text
[pbt] property failed after 41 passed checks and 3005 shrink steps (size 26)
[pbt] utility queue = 1
[pbt] utility wait = 101
[pbt] jobs (SliceOf(IntRange(1, 10))) = []int{3, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 1}
[pbt] workers (IntRange(1, 4)) = 1
[pbt] error: a job waited 101
[pbt] reproduce: go test -run 'TestPool' -pbt.seed=0x1
```

The report lists every utility of the failing case. A passing run lists the best value of each objective in its summary. The objectives share the search steps, so give a run with several of them more steps with `SearchSteps`. A property with a single objective searches exactly as before.

## Searching for slow inputs

A performance property can maximize the elapsed duration of the call under test. Draw the input first, record `time.Now()` immediately before the call, then pass `time.Since(start).Seconds()` to `t.Maximize("seconds", elapsed)`. This keeps generation time out of the utility.

Elapsed time is noisy. Scheduling, garbage collection and caches can change it for the same input. Repeat a slow case before treating it as evidence of a performance bug. A deterministic work count often makes a better search objective.

The guide measures comparisons inside a quadratic scan. Inputs with an early duplicate finish quickly; inputs with many distinct values need more comparisons.

```go
// allDistinct counts the comparisons that this quadratic scan performs.
func allDistinct(xs []int) (bool, int) {
	comparisons := 0
	for i, x := range xs {
		for _, y := range xs[:i] {
			comparisons++
			if x == y {
				return false, comparisons
			}
		}
	}
	return true, comparisons
}

var scanWorkProperty = func(t *pbt.T) {
	xs := pbt.SliceOfN(pbt.IntRange(0, 9), 0, 10).Draw(t, "xs")
	_, comparisons := allDistinct(xs)
	t.Maximize("comparisons", float64(comparisons))
	if comparisons > 20 {
		t.Fatalf("scan used %d comparisons, limit 20", comparisons)
	}
}
```

`TestSearchFindsExpensiveScan` runs this property with `Seed(1)`. Its report is:

```text
[pbt] property failed after 194 passed checks and 213 shrink steps (size 42)
[pbt] utility comparisons = 21
[pbt] xs (SliceOfN(IntRange(0, 9), 0, 10)) = []int{0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 4, 4}
[pbt] error: scan used 21 comparisons, limit 20
[pbt] reproduce: go test -run 'TestScanWork' -pbt.seed=0x1
```

Elapsed time works the same way in a real project: maximize the measured duration and assert the acceptable bound. `Maximize` alone does not fail a case. A passing search reports its best utility but saves no counterexample. The bound makes a slow case fail so that normal runs shrink and save it. The guide's test uses `NoSave` through its recorder to avoid writing the planted failure into the suite.

## Searching with code coverage

`CoverageGuided()` or `-pbt.coverage` enables an experimental search based on `testing.Coverage`. It is off by default. Build with `go test -cover`, and use `-coverpkg` to select the packages whose coverage matters. Without instrumentation, pbt logs a hint and uses ordinary search.

Passing generated cases that increase live block coverage enter a pool of up to 64 seeds. Cases without choices cannot seed mutations. Once the pool has a seed, attempts alternate between a fresh case and a mutation of a randomly selected seed. The pool drops the oldest seed when full and lasts for one `Check` call. Mutations use the seed's size and count toward `Checks` like fresh cases.

This can help with deep chains of comparisons. A case that passes one more comparison reaches another block and can seed attempts at the next comparison. The example recognizes a four-byte header:

```go
// This function lives in a .go file: go test does not instrument _test.go files.
func recognizesHeader(b []byte) bool {
	if len(b) == 4 {
		if b[0] == 'P' {
			if b[1] == 'B' {
				if b[2] == 'T' {
					if b[3] == '!' {
						return true
					}
				}
			}
		}
	}
	return false
}
```

```go
func TestCoverageGuidedHeader(t *testing.T) {
	if testing.CoverMode() == "" {
		t.Skip("run with -cover -coverpkg=go.ymotongpoo.com/pbt/docs/guide/snippets")
	}
	property := func(t *pbt.T) {
		b := pbt.SliceOfN(pbt.SampledFrom([]byte("PBT!?")), 4, 4).Draw(t, "header")
		if got := recognizesHeader(b); got != (string(b) == "PBT!") {
			t.Fatalf("header %q: accepted=%t", b, got)
		}
	}
	logs := passingLogs(t, "TestHeader", property, pbt.Seed(1),
		pbt.Checks(200), pbt.CoverageGuided(), pbt.Verbose())
	mustContain(t, logs, "[pbt] coverage-guided:", "of 200 passing cases", "seeds kept")
}
```

The fixture lives in `coverage_fixture.go`, because Go does not instrument `_test.go` files. The test skips itself when the binary has no instrumentation. Run it alone from the repository root:

```sh
go test -count=1 -v -cover -coverpkg=go.ymotongpoo.com/pbt/docs/guide/snippets ./docs/guide/snippets -run '^TestCoverageGuidedHeader$'
```

The captured output includes:

```text
[pbt] coverage-guided: 4 of 200 passing cases reached new code, 4 seeds kept, coverage 0.0% -> 60.0%
[pbt] OK, passed 200 checks (seed 0x1)
```

The percentages are the live estimate from `testing.Coverage`. They differ from the statement-weighted percentage that `go test` prints at the end. Compiler instrumentation and earlier tests can change the output, so the test checks the report's shape rather than fixed percentages.

Coverage guidance has limits:

- Counters cover the whole process. Earlier tests can exhaust the useful signal, while parallel tests and other goroutines can attribute unrelated coverage to a case.
- The signal describes covered blocks, without edges or execution counts. Comparisons within an already covered block give no new signal.
- Each reading scans the counters, so its cost grows with the instrumented code. Select the packages under test; instrumenting pbt also includes its own work in the signal.
- A seed alone cannot repeat the schedule across different coverage histories. Saved counterexamples still replay their choices normally.

Run a property alone when using this signal, and avoid `t.Parallel`. `Maximize` or `Minimize` takes priority once targeted search starts, with its own `SearchSteps` limit. `CheckExists` ignores coverage guidance.

## Existence

`CheckExists` inverts the question: instead of a property that must hold for every case, it looks for one case where the property holds. A case that fails is a rejected candidate, and the first case that passes is the witness, which pbt shrinks and logs.

```go
// CheckExists succeeds once a case passes: here, a Pythagorean triple. The
// witness is shrunk and logged. The seed keeps the run reproducible: a few
// seeds need more than 5000 cases to meet a triple.
func TestATripleExists(t *testing.T) {
	pbt.CheckExists(t, func(t *pbt.T) {
		a := pbt.IntRange(1, 50).Draw(t, "a")
		b := pbt.IntRange(1, 50).Draw(t, "b")
		c := pbt.IntRange(1, 70).Draw(t, "c")
		if a*a+b*b != c*c {
			t.Fail()
		}
	}, pbt.Checks(5000), pbt.Seed(1))
}
```

```text
[pbt] witness found after 98 rejected cases and 29 shrink steps (seed 0x1) (size 42)
[pbt] a (IntRange(1, 50)) = 3
[pbt] b (IntRange(1, 50)) = 4
[pbt] c (IntRange(1, 70)) = 5
```

The test fails when no witness turns up within the number of checks. `Maximize` works inside `CheckExists` too: a utility that measures the distance to a passing case guides the search toward one. Nothing is saved under `testdata/pbt` for an existential property, since a witness is not a regression.

---

# Generators from types

Writing a generator for every struct of a program is tedious, and most of the time the type already says what the values look like. pbt derives generators from types in two ways: `Make[T]` at run time through reflection, and `cmd/pbtgen` at development time as Go source.

## Make

```go
type Order struct {
	ID       int        `pbt:"min=1"`
	Items    []string   `pbt:"min=1,max=5"`
	Note     string     `pbt:"-"` // stays zero
	Placed   time.Time  `pbt:"min=2026-01-01T00:00:00Z,max=2026-12-31T23:59:59Z"`
	Client   netip.Addr // generated with pbt.Addr
	internal int        // unexported fields stay zero
}

var orderGen = pbt.Make[Order](
	pbt.WithField[Order]("Items", pbt.SliceOfN(pbt.StringN(1, 8), 1, 5)),
)

func TestOrders(t *testing.T) {
	pbt.Check(t, func(t *pbt.T) {
		o := orderGen.Draw(t, "order")
		if o.ID < 1 || len(o.Items) == 0 || o.Note != "" || o.Placed.Year() != 2026 || !o.Client.IsValid() {
			t.Fatalf("unexpected order %+v", o)
		}
	})
}
```

`Make[T]` builds a generator for `T` from its fields, recursively. A `pbt` struct tag adjusts a field: `min` and `max` bound a number or the length of a string, slice or map, and `-` leaves the field zero. Two options replace generators: `WithType(g)` for every value of a type, and `WithField[S](name, g)` for one field of a struct. `Items` gets its non-empty strings from `WithField` above.

`Make` knows the types of the standard library whose state is unexported, and uses the generators of chapter 1 for them.

| Type | Generator |
| --- | --- |
| `time.Time` | `Time`, or `TimeRange` with `min` and `max` |
| `*time.Location` | `FixedZone` |
| `netip.Addr`, `netip.Prefix`, `netip.AddrPort` | `Addr`, `Prefix`, `AddrPort` |
| `net.IP` | addresses of `Addr` in both the 4-byte and the 16-byte form |
| `net.HardwareAddr` | `HardwareAddr` |

A `time.Time` field takes `min` and `max` as RFC 3339 timestamps, as `Placed` does above. `time.Duration` stays an integer type and is drawn like any `int64`.

Other types need help. Unexported fields stay zero, because reflection cannot set them, so a type whose state is all unexported needs `WithType`. Interfaces, channels and functions have no derivable generator and need `WithType` or `WithField` as well; `Make` panics with the field name when one is missing.

`NoPanic` from chapter 4 uses `Make` for the arguments of the function it tests, and accepts the same options.

## Recursive types

A type that contains itself has no finite generator unless something bounds the recursion. `Recursive` gives a leaf generator and a function that extends a generator by one level; the size parameter bounds how many levels a value gets, so a value has about `size` nodes.

```go
// Expr is a recursive type. Recursive bounds the depth with the size
// parameter, so a value has about size nodes instead of growing without end.
type Expr struct {
	Num  int
	Op   string
	Args []Expr
}

var exprGen = pbt.Recursive(
	pbt.Map(pbt.IntRange(0, 9), func(n int) Expr { return Expr{Num: n} }),
	func(self pbt.Gen[Expr]) pbt.Gen[Expr] {
		return pbt.Custom("op", func(t *pbt.T) Expr {
			return Expr{Op: pbt.SampledFrom([]string{"+", "*"}).Draw(t, ""), Args: pbt.SliceOfN(self, 2, 2).Draw(t, "")}
		})
	},
)

func size(e Expr) int {
	n := 1
	for _, a := range e.Args {
		n += size(a)
	}
	return n
}

func TestExprSize(t *testing.T) {
	pbt.Check(t, func(t *pbt.T) {
		e := exprGen.Draw(t, "expr")
		if size(e) > 4*t.Size()+8 {
			t.Fatalf("%d nodes at size %d", size(e), t.Size())
		}
	})
}
```

`Bounded(leaf, node)` is the lower-level form: it keeps one recursion budget per value, shared by every bounded generator drawn while that value is built, which is what two mutually recursive types need.

`Make` bounds the whole value instead. One value gets an allowance of `8*max(size, 1)` units of growth. Every collection element, every rune of a string, every map entry that `Make` tries and every non-nil pointer spends one unit, however deep it sits. When the allowance is spent, collections stop growing and recursive references stay nil or empty. The work of a value therefore grows linearly with the size. Fixed fields, arrays and the minimum lengths of tags are still completed, except where a minimum length would recurse without end.

```go
// A directory holds files and directories. Make shares one allowance of
// growth across the whole value, so a tree stays proportional to the size
// parameter however the fields nest.
type Dir struct {
	Name  string
	Files []string
	Dirs  []Dir
}

func countNodes(d Dir) int {
	n := 1 + len(d.Files) + len([]rune(d.Name))
	for _, s := range d.Files {
		n += len([]rune(s))
	}
	for _, c := range d.Dirs {
		n += countNodes(c)
	}
	return n
}

func TestDirectoryTrees(t *testing.T) {
	pbt.Check(t, func(t *pbt.T) {
		d := pbt.Make[Dir]().Draw(t, "dir")
		if n := countNodes(d); n > 8*max(t.Size(), 1)+1 {
			t.Fatalf("%d elements at size %d", n, t.Size())
		}
	})
}
```

`BoundedGrowth(g)` gives a hand-written generator the same allowance: the collections and pointers drawn inside `g` share it. `UnboundedGrowth(g)` exempts a part from the surrounding allowance, which is what an explicit override needs when its own length rules come first. `Make` uses it for `WithType` and `WithField`.

## pbtgen

`cmd/pbtgen` writes the generators as source, which the compiler checks and which can set unexported fields because the generated file lives in the package itself.

```text
//go:generate go run go.ymotongpoo.com/pbt/cmd/pbtgen -type Order,Customer
```

For each type `T`, `go generate` writes a function `GenT` returning `pbt.Gen[T]` into `pbt_gen.go`. The struct tags of `Make` apply, and a `gen=EXPR` tag names a Go expression to use as the generator of a field, such as a variable of type `pbt.Gen[string]` in the same package. The generated code uses the same standard generators and the same allowance as `Make`, through `BoundedGrowth`. A type without unexported fields therefore gets the same values from both for the same seed, mutually recursive types included. A type with unexported fields gets more from pbtgen, which fills them.

Three flags adjust the output. `-output` names the file. `-prefix` replaces `Gen` in the function names, and pbtgen refuses to write a name that the package already declares, so a hand-written generator is never overwritten. pbtgen reads the files that `go build` would compile on the current platform, so files excluded by build constraints do not affect the generated code.

Choose `Make` when the type changes often or the generator is needed in one test; choose pbtgen when the generator is part of the package's test support, when unexported fields matter, or when a compile error is preferable to a panic at test time.

---

# Standard formats

Many inputs of a program are strings in a format that a standard defines: timestamps, e-mail addresses, URIs, JSON, UUIDs, language tags. The package `go.ymotongpoo.com/pbt/format` generates them. Every generator returns a `pbt.Gen[string]` and builds its values from the grammar of the standard. Every value is valid, including the values the shrinker tries.

```go
import "go.ymotongpoo.com/pbt/format"
```

The generators of chapter 1 return Go types, such as a `time.Time` or a `netip.Addr`. The generators of this package return text. `pbt.IPv6()` gives an address; `format.RFC4291IPv6()` gives the ways to write one.

## Two names for two questions

A format raises two questions. What should a program write? What must a parser accept? The answers differ, and the package gives each one its own name.

- A function with a plain name, such as `Email`, `URL` or `HTTPDate`, generates the common or canonical form. Use it for the input of code that produces or stores the format, and for values that should pass every validator.
- A function named after a standard, such as `RFC5321Mailbox`, `RFC3986URI` or `RFC9110HTTPDate`, generates the alternatives of the standard's production. Use it to test a parser. It leaves out only what the standard forbids generators to produce, such as the obsolete syntax of RFC 5322. Its documentation names those parts and the bounds it puts on open lengths.

`Time(layout)` takes the layout constants of package `time`, so `format.Time(time.RFC1123)` generates what `time.Time.Format` writes for that layout. It is the alias for what Go writes; `RFC3339` is the alias for what RFC 3339 allows.

| Area | What a program writes | What a parser must accept |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timestamps | `Time(time.RFC3339)`, `HTTPDate` | `RFC3339`, `RFC3339FullDate`, `RFC3339FullTime`, `RFC9110HTTPDate`, `RFC5322DateTime` |
| Durations | `ISO8601Duration` | `RFC3339Duration` |
| Addresses | `IPv4`, `RFC5952IPv6`, `CIDR`, `MAC` | `RFC4291IPv6` |
| Host names | `Hostname`, `IDNAHostname`, `UnicodeHostname` | `RFC1035Domain` |
| E-mail | `Email`, `HTMLEmail`, `SMTPUTF8Mailbox` | `RFC5321Mailbox`, `RFC5322AddrSpec` |
| URIs | `URL` | `RFC3986URI`, `RFC3986Reference` |
| HTTP | `HTTPToken`, `HTTPFieldName`, `HTTPFieldValue`, `MediaType` | `RFC9110FieldValue`, `RFC9110MediaType`, `RFC6265Cookie`, `RFC6265SetCookie` |
| Data | `JSON`, `IJSON`, `JSONPointer`, `JSONPointerFragment`, `UUID`, `SemVer`, `LanguageTag` | `RFC4180CSV`, `RFC5646LanguageTag` |
| Encodings | `Base64`, `Base64URL`, `Base32`, `Base32Hex`, `Base16`, `Hex` and the unpadded `Raw` forms | |
| Numbers | `PhoneNumber`, `PaymentCard`, `ISBN13`, `ISBN10` | |

## Testing a parser

A property that feeds a parser every form of its standard finds where the parser departs from it. Every RFC 3339 timestamp should parse with the layout of the same name.

```go
// Every timestamp of RFC 3339 should parse with the RFC3339 layout of
// package time.
var rfc3339Property = func(t *pbt.T) {
	s := format.RFC3339().Draw(t, "")
	if _, err := time.Parse(time.RFC3339, s); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("time.Parse rejects %s: %v", s, err)
	}
}
```

```text
[pbt] property failed after 1 passed checks and 19 shrink steps (size 2)
[pbt] s (RFC3339()) = "1970-01-01T00:00:00z"
[pbt] error: time.Parse rejects 1970-01-01T00:00:00z: parsing time "1970-01-01T00:00:00z" as "2006-01-02T15:04:05Z07:00": cannot parse "z" as "Z07:00"
[pbt] reproduce: go test -run 'TestRFC3339' -pbt.seed=0x1
```

RFC 3339 allows a lower-case `z` and `t`, and `time.Parse` rejects them, as it rejects the leap second `23:59:60`. Whether that matters depends on where your timestamps come from. The property makes the decision visible, and the shrunk case shows the difference in one character. The documentation of each generator lists the differences between the standard and the parsers of Go's standard library, as measured on Go 1.26, and names the releases where a difference changed: `url.Parse` accepts IPvFuture literals such as `http://[v1.x]/` up to Go 1.25.1 and rejects them from Go 1.25.2. The tests of the package pin the differences on every supported version of Go.

## Testing what a program writes

For the input of a program, the plain names give values that every reasonable consumer accepts. A sign-up form can store `format.Email()` and expect `net/mail` to read the same address back.

```go
// A sign-up form stores the address it receives, and the confirmation mail
// must reach the same mailbox.
func TestSignupAddresses(t *testing.T) {
	pbt.Check(t, func(t *pbt.T) {
		email := format.Email().Draw(t, "email")
		addr, err := mail.ParseAddress(email)
		if err != nil || addr.Address != email {
			t.Fatalf("mail.ParseAddress(%q) = %v, %v", email, addr, err)
		}
	})
}
```

The generators lean toward the cases that break code, as the generators of chapter 1 do. In a share of the cases:

- `Email` makes local parts of exactly 64 characters, and `Hostname` makes names of exactly 253.
- `RFC3339` writes leap seconds and the offset `-00:00`.
- `JSON` writes numbers far beyond 64 bits and unpaired surrogate escapes.

The documentation of each generator says how often.

```go
func TestDecoders(t *testing.T) {
	pbt.Check(t, func(t *pbt.T) {
		doc := format.JSON().Draw(t, "doc")
		if !json.Valid([]byte(doc)) {
			t.Fatalf("json.Valid rejects %s", doc)
		}
		link := format.URL().Draw(t, "link")
		u, err := url.Parse(link)
		if err != nil || u.Host == "" {
			t.Fatalf("url.Parse(%q) = %v, %v", link, u, err)
		}
		at := format.Time(time.RFC1123Z).Draw(t, "at")
		if _, err := time.Parse(time.RFC1123Z, at); err != nil {
			t.Fatal(err)
		}
	})
}
```

## How the values shrink

Values shrink toward short valid strings: `a@a.aa` for `Email`, `http://a` for `URL`, `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z` for `RFC3339`, `null` for `JSON`. The shrinker prefers fewer choices, so a part can also shrink within the alternative it started from. A quoted local part, for example, shrinks toward the empty quoted string, `""@a`. The documentation of each generator lists the targets of every alternative.

## What the package leaves out

The package generates syntax, not registered values.

- A language tag is well-formed, but its subtags are not checked against the IANA registry.
- A payment card number has a correct check digit, but no issuer assigned it.
- An ISBN is not hyphenated, since the hyphens depend on ranges that the ISBN agency publishes.

The package has no tables that follow a registry, such as the country codes of ISO 3166 or the currencies of ISO 4217, because they change with the registry. Write them with `SampledFrom` over the values your program supports.

---

# Where to go next

## The examples

The `examples` module of the repository ports every chapter of the book [PropEr Testing](https://propertesting.com/) by Fred Hebert to Go. The book is the best long-form introduction to the way of thinking behind pbt, and the ports show how each of its Erlang examples reads in Go.

| Book chapter | Package | Shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 to 4 | `ch01cash`, `ch04stateless` | first properties, modeling, the exercises on lists |
| 5 | `ch05generators` | custom generators, `Collect` and `Aggregate`, recursive and `Sized` generators |
| 6 | `ch06birthday` | a CSV round trip, templates, example tests next to properties |
| 7 | `ch07checkout` | layered `Bind`, negative tests, discovering a specification bug |
| 8 | `ch08shrinking` | `ShrinkTo`, `LetShrink`, `SampleShrink` |
| 9 | `ch09cache` | a sequential and a parallel stateful test of a cache |
| 10 | `ch10bookstore` | a stateful test against a database, with SQLite and PostgreSQL |
| 11 | `ch11breaker` | a state machine with the `fsm` package |

Each package has a README that answers the exercises of its chapter. Run them with `go test ./...` inside `examples`.

## Practical examples

The `examples/practical` directory tests small but realistic systems the way a project would: through their public API, against a model, with a planted bug whose report the tests check. The examples build on chapters 5 to 7.

| Package | System | Shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `httpapi` | a REST API with optimistic concurrency, served by `httptest` | server-assigned ids as `Var`s, status codes as postconditions, a parallel run against a server that allocates ids outside its lock |
| `jobqueue` | a worker queue with leases, a visibility timeout and dead letters | a fake clock advanced by a command, stale leases kept in the model, an ack that does not check its lease, `Causality` on a handoff between two workers |
| `ratelimit` | a sliding-window limiter per client | the rule "at most N requests in any window" as the model, a sweep that forgets clients too early, a budgeted run whose `ReportJSON` and `Observations` files a test reads the way a CI job would |
| `sessions` | a session store with expiry, refresh and logout | the `fsm` package with state data and a clock, time as a transition split by where it leads |
| `ledger` | transfers between accounts | a model next to an audit that checks only the invariants, an overdraft race caught in parallel, `Signature` and `MaxFailures` reporting two causes of the audit apart |

Run `go test -v -run Caught ./practical/...` inside `examples` to read the reports of the planted bugs. The README of the directory describes the patterns the examples share.

## The examples of the discovery guide

The directory [examples/discovery](https://github.com/ymotongpoo/pbt/tree/main/examples/discovery) holds a Go port of the examples of the Japanese book 『プロパティはどう思いつくのか　プロパティベーステスト発見ガイド』 (work in progress) by Yoshi Yamaguchi, whose own listings use fast-check. Where the guide explains what each function of pbt does, the book is about finding the properties to write: it derives them from a specification, chapter by chapter, from example tests and algebraic laws to state machines, concurrency and the statistics of a run. Each property is checked against planted bugs.

A test whose name ends in `Mutant` runs a property against a planted bug and is supposed to fail, so it skips itself unless `PBT_MUTANTS` is set. Run `go test -race ./discovery/...` inside `examples` for the ordinary tests, and `./discovery/run_mutants.sh` to check that every planted bug is caught. The README of the directory lists the chapters.

## Coming from rapid

[MIGRATION.md](https://github.com/ymotongpoo/pbt/blob/main/MIGRATION.md) maps rapid's API onto pbt, table by table, and lists what pbt adds. Most rapid tests translate line by line; the stateful tests change shape, because pbt generates the whole sequence against the model before running it. [BENCHMARK.md](https://github.com/ymotongpoo/pbt/blob/main/BENCHMARK.md) compares the two libraries on the same properties.

## Reference material

- The [package documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/go.ymotongpoo.com/pbt) on pkg.go.dev describes every function and option, with runnable examples.
- The documentation of [package format](https://pkg.go.dev/go.ymotongpoo.com/pbt/format) describes every format, the parts of its standard that it covers, and its shrink targets.
- [DESIGN.md](https://github.com/ymotongpoo/pbt/blob/main/DESIGN.md) records the design decisions and the comparison with PropEr, QuickCheck, Hypothesis, rapid and Hegel, with a Japanese version in DESIGN.ja.md.
- [CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/ymotongpoo/pbt/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) lists the changes of each release. The API may still change before v1.0.
- Issues and questions go to the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/ymotongpoo/pbt).

## Flags at a glance

```text
go test ./... -pbt.checks=1000          # more cases
go test ./... -pbt.seed=0x1c3           # repeat a run
go test ./... -pbt.startsize=10 -pbt.maxsize=100
go test ./... -pbt.shrinktime=2m
go test ./... -pbt.checks=1000000 -pbt.budget=30s # time-limited search
go test ./... -pbt.searchsteps=5000     # longer targeted searches
go test ./... -pbt.failures=3           # collect up to three distinct failures
go test ./... -pbt.causality=32         # continuations per sequential prefix
go test ./... -pbt.warnhealth=duplicate # warn about repeated choices
go test ./... -pbt.checkhealth=default  # fail on wasted or oversized input
go test ./... -pbt.ignorehealth=slow    # hide the timing warning
go test ./... -pbt.nosave               # keep testdata/pbt untouched
go test ./... -pbt.replay=testdata/pbt/TestQueue/3f2a… -run TestQueue
go test ./... -pbt.v                    # summaries and shrink steps
go test ./... -pbt.json=runs.jsonl       # one JSON line per run
go test ./... -pbt.observe=observations  # OpenPBTStats files for Tyche
go test -cover -coverpkg=./... ./... -pbt.coverage # guide with live block coverage
```

---

# Testing a project with an agent

Start with a small set of properties whose failures would matter to the project. Keep each property, its source of expected behaviour, and its results together. A useful result is a reproducible disagreement with the project's contract, supported by a test that preserves the evidence.

## Establish the contract

Read the documentation, public types, existing tests and fixtures for the code under test. Look for standards that the project promises to follow. These sources define valid inputs, allowed errors and expected results. Record disagreements between them before choosing an oracle.

Basic rules can also supply properties: valid requests should not panic, stored data should not disappear, and operations should finish. State the limits of each rule. For example, a documented panic on invalid input does not violate a promise about valid input.

Choose a few places where a bug would cause the most harm. For each, write down the input domain, the expected result, and the source that requires it. Quote the relevant sentence when one exists. If the contract remains ambiguous, identify the missing decision instead of inventing a requirement.

## Choose an oracle

An oracle decides whether the observed result is correct. Start with an inexpensive one, then add an independent check where it would catch a different kind of error.

| Oracle, roughly by effort | Property and pbt tools |
| --- | --- |
| No panic | Use [NoPanic](04-properties.md#panics) to generate function arguments from types, or call the function inside `Check`; a panic fails the case. |
| Round trip | Generate a value with `ForAll` or `Draw`, encode it, decode it, and compare with `Fatalf`. Account for documented normalization. See [generators](01-generators.md) and [formats](10-formats.md). |
| Reference model | Keep a small model of expected state and compare operations through [Commands and postconditions](05-stateful.md). Reset the system for each case. |
| Invariants after every step | Check conservation, ordering or ownership in each command's `Post`. Remember that `Post` sees the model before `Next`. |
| Metamorphic check | Draw one input, transform it, and compare the related results in one property. For example, a documented order-independent operation should survive a permutation. |
| Differential check | Send the same drawn input to two independent implementations and compare results with `Fatalf`. First establish that their contracts agree on that input domain. |

For a possible hang, set `go test -timeout`. The [Deadline combinator](04-properties.md#combining-properties) checks elapsed time only after the call returns. A difference between two implementations is evidence to investigate, not proof that either particular implementation is wrong.

## Build inputs that exercise the contract

Prefer [generators that construct valid inputs](01-generators.md) over a broad generator followed by `Filter` or `Assume`. Use `Bind` for dependent fields and `Frequency` for the mix of alternatives. Include boundaries from existing tests and fixtures alongside generated values. Keep invalid-input properties separate so that their expected errors remain explicit.

Use the [format package](10-formats.md) for standard text inputs. Check whether the project accepts the full standard grammar or only its common form. Use [Make or pbtgen](09-types.md) for Go types, with field overrides for constraints that types cannot express.

Generate [command sequences](05-stateful.md) for stateful code. Independent calls rarely reach states such as expired leases or a closed queue with pending work. Change the model only in `init` and `Next`; let the generator and checks read it. Reset external state, clocks and resources for every execution, including shrinking and diagnostic replays.

Measure the distribution with [Classify, Cover and CheckCoverage](02-distribution.md). Label important operations and boundary cases. Require a minimum share when missing that class would invalidate the experiment. Inspect health warnings before increasing the number of checks. Enable `WarnHealth(HealthDuplicate)` when repeated choices would waste a large search.

## Run in stages

First compile and run the affected package with the default 100 checks. Inspect the statistics and any warnings. Then increase the case count and try several recorded seeds. The following commands assume a property named `TestQueue` in the current package:

```sh
go test -count=1 -run '^TestQueue$' -pbt.v
go test -count=1 -run '^TestQueue$' -pbt.checks=10000 -pbt.seed=1
go test -count=1 -run '^TestQueue$' -pbt.checks=10000 -pbt.seed=2
go test -count=1 -run '^TestQueue$' -pbt.checks=1000000 -pbt.budget=30s -pbt.seed=3
```

[Budget](04-properties.md#time-budgets) caps search time, while the case limit can end it earlier. For targeted properties, increase `-pbt.searchsteps`. Neither setting interrupts a blocked call.

Use `-pbt.failures=3` to collect several causes in one run. Assign stable [Signature names](03-shrinking.md#the-failure-stays-the-same) when causes share an assertion site. Read `-pbt.json=runs.jsonl` for structured run results instead of parsing console text. Use `-pbt.observe=observations` for [OpenPBTStats records that Tyche reads](04-properties.md#machine-readable-output).

Try [CoverageGuided](08-targeted.md#searching-with-code-coverage) when nested comparisons make random progress difficult:

```sh
go test -count=1 -run '^TestQueue$' -cover -coverpkg=./... -pbt.coverage -pbt.checks=10000
```

Select the packages under test with `-coverpkg`. Run the property alone and avoid parallel tests because coverage counters belong to the whole process. Coverage guidance does not supply an oracle; the property still needs assertions.

## Investigate a failure

Keep the saved case under `testdata/pbt` and run the report's `reproduce:` command. Use `-pbt.replay=FILE` to replay a particular saved case. Record the Go, pbt and project versions: generator changes can change the meaning of saved choices. Inspect a `HealthStale` warning before treating replay as the original input.

Add the minimal input to an ordinary regression test when that makes the defect easier to inspect. Confirm that it fails against the unchanged code. For a sequential stateful failure, [Causality](05-stateful.md#finding-the-step-that-caused-a-failure) can suggest an earlier command that made the failure likely. Its sampled rates guide investigation; they do not establish the cause by themselves.

| Verdict | Signs | Next action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Real bug | A valid input produces a result that contradicts the recorded contract. | Preserve the reproducer and report the mismatch. Fix the implementation only within the requested scope. |
| Test bug | The generator violates a precondition, the model leaks state, or the comparison assumes an undocumented rule. | Correct that specific mistake, record the reason, and rerun the affected properties. |
| Intended behaviour | Documentation or an existing test explicitly permits this result. | Adjust the expectation to the contract and keep a test of the documented behaviour. |
| Environment | The result depends on a clock, platform, service, missing tool or resource limit. | Record the dependency, control it where possible, and rerun before assigning the defect to the library. |

Check related existing findings and issues to avoid reporting the same cause twice. Preserve the original observation when a controlled rerun behaves differently. State what remains uncertain.

## Extend a passing test

A passing run covers the generated cases and the assertions that ran. Use its evidence to choose the next change:

- Inspect labels and command statistics for missing shapes or states. Change weights or add a generator branch, then measure again.
- Inspect code coverage with `go test -cover -coverprofile=coverage.out`, then `go tool cover -func=coverage.out`. Trace uncovered paths back to missing inputs or operations.
- Add a new oracle on the same code. A round trip can pass while both directions share a bug; an independent model may reveal it.
- Count what `Assume`, `Filter` and explicit exclusions remove. Check whether an exclusion hides the cases that matter.
- Raise `-pbt.maxsize` for longer inputs or programs, while watching generation cost. Try another seed and record the result.
- Move to another part of the project when further changes no longer improve the tested inputs or assertions.

## Preserve the evidence

Never weaken or delete a property to make a failure disappear. Correct a mistaken oracle only with evidence from the contract. Never delete a saved case to make a run pass. Do not change the code under test until a failing test demonstrates the defect.

A bug report includes the tested versions, minimal input, exact commands, expected result and actual result. Include the documentation sentence that requires the expected behaviour. If a type or standard supplies the rule, identify that source instead. Report how many cases ran, which properties failed, the triage verdict, and any untested scope. Keep the reproducer with the report so that another person can check the finding.
